title: History of astronomy: how people changed their minds about who moves, the Earth or the sky

summary.text: Every sky-watcher in history saw the same thing: the Sun rises, crosses the sky and sets, while the ground stays still. Yet in the year 499, Aryabhata wrote that the ground is what turns. How could anyone tell? Your child sits in a spinning chair with eyes shut and finds out how little a steady turn can be felt. She lights a ball with a lamp to repeat what Galileo saw when he pointed a telescope at Venus. She tests how finely she can measure an angle, as Tycho Brahe did, and meets the small gap of 8 arcminutes that made Kepler give up perfect circles. Along the way come the giant stone dials of Jaipur, the first Indian ideas about a Sun at the centre, and why a sundial and a phone never quite agree.
summary.art: A child in a swivel chair with her eyes shut in the middle of a room, and around the walls faint pictures of a Jaipur stone sundial, a telescope, a brass quadrant and a planet making a loop among the stars.

intro.hook: Close your eyes in a smooth, steadily turning chair. Can you tell that you are turning? Open your eyes, and the room seems to spin round you. So who is really turning, you or the room? And what does that have to do with the Sun and the Earth?
intro.text: For thousands of years, people looked up and saw the Sun and the stars move round them. A few said the Earth must be the one that turns. Nobody could feel it. In this unit you sit in a spinning chair and try to feel a steady turn. You make a lamp and a ball show the phases of Venus. You build a quadrant and find how exactly you can measure an angle. You draw an ellipse with string and pins. And you learn how an 8-arcminute gap in a table of numbers changed astronomy.
intro.art: A girl on a swivel chair with a scarf over her eyes, a parent holding the back of the chair, and sheets of paper stuck on the walls all around the room.

outcomes: I can explain why a steady turn or a steady movement cannot be felt, and why the Sun seems to go round us even though the Earth is what turns.
I can say why planets such as Mars sometimes seem to slide backwards among the stars, and how an Earth-centred and a Sun-centred model each explained it.
I can use a lamp and a ball to show that the phases of Venus cannot all be explained if Venus stays between the Earth and the Sun.
I can say what 'precision' means for a measurement, and show from my own readings that a steadier, longer instrument gives readings that agree more closely.
I can describe how Kepler used Tycho's careful readings to show that planets move on ellipses, and draw an ellipse with a loop of string.
I can explain why a sundial tilted at my city's latitude shows the Sun's time, and why it differs from my phone's clock.
I can name Aryabhata, Nilakantha, Copernicus, Kepler, Galileo and at least two women astronomers, and say one thing that each found out.

terms.meaning: A big world that goes round a star. The word comes from the Greek for 'wanderer', because planets drift among the fixed stars from night to night.
terms.example: Mars, Jupiter and Venus are planets that can be seen without a telescope.
terms.art: A night sky with fixed stars and a bright planet with a dotted line showing where it was on the nights before.

terms.meaning: The time when a planet seems to stop, slide backwards among the stars for a few weeks, and then go forward again.
terms.example: Mars seems to move backwards for about two months, about every 26 months.
terms.art: A zigzag loop drawn among the stars, with a planet at the middle of the loop.

terms.meaning: A small circle on a big circle. Ptolemy used epicycles to explain why planets seem to loop in the sky.
terms.example: In Ptolemy's model, Mars sat on a small circle, and the small circle itself went round the Earth.
terms.art: A big circle round the Earth and a small circle riding on it, with a planet on the small circle and a looped path.

terms.meaning: Having the Earth at the centre. A geocentric model says that the Sun, Moon and planets go round the Earth.
terms.example: Ptolemy's model of the sky was geocentric.
terms.art: The Earth in the middle with the Sun, Moon and planets on circles round it.

terms.meaning: Having the Sun at the centre. A heliocentric model says that the planets, including the Earth, go round the Sun.
terms.example: Copernicus put the Sun at the centre in 1543.
terms.art: The Sun in the middle with the Earth and other planets on circles round it.

terms.meaning: A shape like a stretched circle, an oval. It has two special points inside it called foci.
terms.example: Each planet goes round the Sun on an ellipse, with the Sun at one focus.
terms.art: An oval with two dots marked inside it and a loop of string round them.

terms.meaning: A very small angle. There are 60 arcminutes in one degree. The Moon is about 30 arcminutes wide in the sky.
terms.example: Tycho Brahe measured the places of planets to about one arcminute without a telescope.
terms.art: A circle divided into degrees, with one degree enlarged into 60 tiny parts.

terms.meaning: A tool for measuring how high something is in the sky. It is a quarter of a circle with a scale of degrees and a way to sight along an edge.
terms.example: Tycho Brahe had a huge brass quadrant, with a radius of about two metres.
terms.art: A quarter-circle of wood and brass with a sighting edge and a hanging weight on a thread.

terms.meaning: A round brass instrument, often hand-sized, for measuring the height of the Sun or a star and for working out the time and the direction.
terms.example: Mahendra Suri wrote the first surviving Sanskrit book on the astrolabe about 1370.
terms.art: A round brass disc with a ring to hang it, a rotating pointer and engraved scales.

terms.meaning: The part of a sundial that casts the shadow. It can be a stick, a wall or a stone stairway.
terms.example: The stairway of the great Samrat Yantra in Jaipur is a gnomon.
terms.art: A tilted stick on a flat plate with its shadow falling across hour lines.

terms.meaning: How far north or south a place is from the equator, measured in degrees. It is also the height of the Pole Star above the horizon.
terms.example: Chennai is at about 13 degrees north. Jaipur is at about 27 degrees north.
terms.art: A globe with the equator and a line of latitude for a city, and a person looking at the Pole Star.

terms.meaning: The moment when the Sun is highest in the sky at your place, and shadows point exactly north or south.
terms.example: Local noon in Kolkata comes about an hour before local noon in Jaipur.
terms.art: A stick at midday with its shortest shadow lying along a north-south line.

terms.meaning: One clock time used across a whole country. India's Standard Time is based on the Sun at 82.5 degrees east.
terms.example: Your phone shows Indian Standard Time, even in Jaipur, where the Sun reaches its highest point about 27 minutes later.
terms.art: A map of India with a vertical line at 82.5 degrees east and clocks in Jaipur and Kolkata.

terms.meaning: How closely repeated readings of the same thing agree with each other. Small spread means high precision.
terms.example: Ten readings of an angle that all lie between 26 and 28 degrees are more precise than ten that lie between 20 and 34.
terms.art: Two dartboards, one with darts bunched together and one with darts scattered.

terms.meaning: Venus changes its lit shape like the Moon, from a thin crescent to nearly full, and it also changes its size as it gets closer or farther.
terms.example: Galileo saw this through his telescope in 1610.
terms.art: A row of Venus shapes from a big thin crescent to a small full disc.

terms.meaning: The small shift in where a near thing seems to be, when you look at it from two places.
terms.example: In 1838, Friedrich Bessel measured the tiny parallax of a star as the Earth moved round the Sun.
terms.art: A finger seen against a wall from the left eye and the right eye, in two different places.

terms.meaning: A way of picturing how something works, which can be tested against what we see. Models can be drawn, built or written as numbers.
terms.example: Ptolemy's circles and Kepler's ellipses are two models of the planets.
terms.art: A small cardboard model of the Sun and planets on circles next to a drawing of the same circles.

terms.meaning: A year with an extra day, 29 February, added to keep the calendar in step with the seasons.
terms.example: 2024 was a leap year. 1900 was not.
terms.art: A calendar page for February with a 29th day circled in red.

explanations.concept: The wandering stars and their backward loops
explanations.definition: Planets are the 'wandering stars'. Over weeks they move among the fixed stars, and every so often a planet seems to slow, stop, slide backwards and then go forward again.
explanations.description: Most stars keep their places from night to night. A few bright lights do not. The ancient Greeks called them planets, which means wanderers. Mars moves eastwards among the stars for many months. Then it slows, stops and slides backwards for about two months, before it turns and goes forward again. This happens about every 26 months. For people who thought the Earth stood still, this was a puzzle. A planet moving in a plain circle round us would never go backwards. About 150 CE, Ptolemy explained it with epicycles. Each planet sat on a small circle, and the small circle went round the Earth. The maths worked well enough to predict where planets would be for more than a thousand years.
examples: The loop of Mars happens every 26 months or so, and the Babylonians and Indians recorded it.
Ptolemy's book, which the Arabs called the Almagest, gave tables for every planet.
A planet is brightest in the middle of its loop, when it is closest to the Earth.
explanations.art: A zigzag path of Mars among stars over several months, with arrows to show forward, backward and forward again.
explanations.context: This card is about the puzzle that started the long argument: why do planets sometimes move backwards?

explanations.concept: Who moves? Aryabhata and the boat
explanations.definition: In 499, the Indian astronomer Aryabhata wrote that the Earth spins once a day, and that the stars only seem to move westwards.
explanations.description: Aryabhata was twenty-three when he wrote his book, the Aryabhatiya. He wrote that a person in a boat moving forwards sees the still things on the bank moving backwards. In the same way, he said, people on the Earth see the still stars moving westwards, while it is the Earth that turns eastwards. He also wrote that eclipses are shadows. The idea was bold, because nobody could feel the Earth turn. Brahmagupta, another great astronomer, argued against it in 628. He asked why birds flying up from a tree can find the tree again, if the ground is racing away under them. Most Indian astronomers kept the old view for centuries. But the question stayed alive, and was asked again later in Kerala and elsewhere.
examples: When a smooth train pulls out of a station, the platform of the next train seems to slide backwards.
In a boat on a still river, the trees on the bank seem to move.
Al-Biruni, who studied Indian astronomy about the year 1000, wrote that the idea of a spinning Earth could not be disproved by the maths of the time.
explanations.art: A person sitting in a boat on a river looking at trees on the bank that seem to slide backwards, with an arrow showing the boat's own movement.
explanations.context: This card is about the first clear Indian statement that the Earth spins, and about the objection to it.

explanations.concept: Why a steady turn cannot be felt
explanations.definition: You feel changes in your movement, such as starting, stopping and turning corners. You do not feel a steady movement at all.
explanations.description: In a smooth aeroplane, flying at 800 kilometres an hour, you can pour a cup of tea as if you were sitting at home. You feel the engines starting and the bumps, but not the speed. Galileo described this in 1632 with a ship: in a cabin below deck, with no window, nothing you do shows whether the ship is still or moving smoothly. The Earth turns once in 24 hours. At the equator, the ground moves at about 1,670 kilometres an hour. At Chennai it moves at about 1,630. But it never starts or stops, and it turns very gently, so we feel nothing. The Earth's own spin is the steadiest motion we know.
examples: A passenger on a smooth, steady train cannot tell with eyes shut if it is moving, until the train brakes or turns.
The Earth also goes round the Sun at about 30 kilometres a second, and we feel none of it.
A lift feels heavier or lighter only while it starts or stops.
explanations.art: A girl calmly drinking tea on an aeroplane with a speed arrow outside, and a cabin with no window.
explanations.context: This card explains why nobody could feel the Earth turn, and why that did not prove that it stood still.

explanations.concept: A Sun at the centre: Nilakantha and Copernicus
explanations.definition: A heliocentric model puts the Sun at the centre of the planets' paths. In Kerala about 1500, and in Poland in 1543, astronomers made models in which the planets go round the Sun.
explanations.description: Nilakantha Somayaji, an astronomer of Kerala, wrote a book called the Tantrasangraha about 1500. In his model, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter and Saturn go round the Sun, and the Sun goes round the Earth. This explained the odd behaviour of the planets in a neat way. In 1543, the Polish astronomer Nicolaus Copernicus went further. In his book he put the Sun at the centre and made the Earth a planet that spins and goes round it. Copernicus still used circles, and still needed small extra circles to match the sky. At first his model was no more accurate than Ptolemy's. It won people over slowly, because it explained why planets loop. The loop is Earth overtaking a slower, outer planet, as a car overtakes a lorry. And the Sun-centred model made the planets' sizes and orders follow in a simple way.
examples: Tycho Brahe later made a middle model, in which the planets go round the Sun and the Sun goes round the Earth. Nilakantha's is similar.
The loops of Mars seen from the faster Earth are like a lorry that seems to slide backwards while you overtake it.
Copernicus kept his idea to himself for years, and his book appeared in print only in 1543, the year he died.
explanations.art: The Sun in the middle with the planets on circles, and the Earth passing Mars on the inside, with a dotted line to the stars showing Mars's loop.
explanations.context: This card is about the first models with a Sun at the centre, from India and from Poland.

explanations.concept: Tycho, Kepler and the end of perfect circles
explanations.definition: Kepler used Tycho Brahe's careful readings of Mars to show that planets move on ellipses, not on circles.
explanations.description: Tycho Brahe, a Danish nobleman, built the finest instruments of his day and used them for 20 years. His readings of planets were accurate to about one arcminute, and no telescope had yet been invented. After he died in 1601, his assistant Johannes Kepler worked on the readings for Mars. Kepler tried many circles. At last he found one that matched Tycho's readings to within 8 arcminutes. But Tycho's readings were never wrong by that much. Kepler wrote that he could not ignore 8 arcminutes. He threw out the circle. In 1609 he published his discovery: Mars goes round the Sun on an ellipse, with the Sun at one focus. Later he found that a planet moves faster when it is closer to the Sun, and that planets farther out take longer for a lap.
examples: Eight arcminutes is about one quarter of the width of the full Moon.
Mars's ellipse is so close to a circle that you can hardly see the difference. Only the Sun's off-centre place shows it.
The Earth's own path is even closer to a circle, and it is a little nearer the Sun in early January than in July.
explanations.art: A circle and an ellipse drawn over each other, nearly the same, with a tiny gap marked '8 arcminutes' and the Sun slightly off-centre.
explanations.context: This card is about how a very small gap in careful readings ended 2,000 years of belief in circles.

explanations.definition: In 1609 and 1610, Galileo used a telescope to show things in the sky that an Earth-centred sky could not easily explain: moons going round Jupiter, and the phases of Venus.
explanations.description: Galileo heard of the Dutch telescope in 1609, and made much better ones. In January 1610, he saw four small lights near Jupiter that changed places from night to night and went with the planet. They were moons going round Jupiter. So not everything went round the Earth. In late 1610 he watched Venus change from a small round disc to a big thin crescent over months. If Venus always stayed between the Earth and the Sun, it could only show crescents. Showing a nearly full disc meant it could also go behind the Sun. So Venus goes round the Sun. This did not prove that the Earth moves, because Tycho's middle model also fitted. But it killed Ptolemy's Venus. He also saw mountains and craters on the Moon, and far more stars in the Milky Way than anyone had known.
examples: Venus looks about six times wider when it is nearest to us than when it is farthest.
The four large moons of Jupiter are still called the Galilean moons.
Galileo's drawings of the Moon in 1610 show craters with shadows, the same way you see in your own eyes with a small telescope.
explanations.art: A row of Venus shapes from a small full disc to a large crescent, and four tiny dots beside Jupiter on three different nights.
explanations.context: This card is about the first telescope discoveries and why Venus mattered.

explanations.definition: It took until the 1700s and 1800s to find direct evidence that the Earth goes round the Sun and spins.
explanations.description: In 1729, James Bradley found that every star seems to make a tiny yearly circle in the sky, because the Earth is moving through starlight, as rain seems to slant when you run. In 1838, Friedrich Bessel found the tiny parallax of a star called 61 Cygni. It seems to shift as the Earth goes round its orbit. The shift told him that the star is about 11 light-years away. In 1851, Léon Foucault hung a heavy pendulum on a long wire in Paris. Its swing slowly turned round the floor over the hours. The pendulum kept swinging in the same direction, while the Earth turned under it. Today, spacecraft see the Earth spin and go round the Sun.
examples: A Foucault pendulum in Paris turns its swing about 11 degrees every hour. Near the equator it would not turn at all.
Bessel's star shifted by less than the width of a coin seen from 5 kilometres away.
Each of these proofs was made possible by better and more precise instruments.
explanations.art: A heavy pendulum on a long wire swinging over a floor marked with a circle of pegs, with the swing slowly changing direction.
explanations.context: This card is about the first direct evidence that the Earth moves, found long after Aryabhata and Copernicus.

explanations.definition: Before telescopes, the finer an instrument's scale, the more exactly it could measure an angle. A bigger instrument can have finer divisions that are easier to read.
explanations.description: A quadrant that is a hand wide has a scale you can read to about one degree. A quadrant two metres wide has a scale where one arcminute is a few millimetres long. That is why Tycho built enormous brass instruments. From 1724 to about 1737, Raja Sawai Jai Singh II built five observatories in India, called the Jantar Mantar, at Delhi, Jaipur, Ujjain, Varanasi and Mathura. The Samrat Yantra at Jaipur is a stairway about 27 metres high that works as a sundial, and its shadow edge creeps along the scale at about six centimetres a minute. Jai Singh built in stone because brass instruments bent and wore. Ulugh Beg built a huge observatory at Samarkand in the 1420s, with an arc made in a trench in the ground.
examples: A stone instrument cannot warp like a thin brass one, so it keeps its shape.
The Jaipur Samrat Yantra is still used to tell the local time, and it is within a minute or two.
Even a huge sundial has a blurry shadow edge, because the Sun is a disc and not a point.
explanations.art: A tiny brass quadrant held in a hand beside a giant stone stairway sundial with a person climbing it.
explanations.context: This card is about why astronomers built huge instruments, from Tycho's brass to Jai Singh's stone.

explanations.concept: Astrolabes and observatories across the Islamic world and India
explanations.definition: From about 800 to 1500, astronomers in Baghdad, Cairo, Samarkand and India built observatories, improved the astrolabe and kept long records of the sky.
explanations.description: Astronomers wrote in Arabic, Persian and Sanskrit, and often learned from each other's books. Al-Biruni, who worked about the year 1000, measured the size of the Earth by climbing a mountain and measuring the dip of the horizon. He also wrote a book about India and its astronomy. A woman known as al-Ijliyya, often called Mariam al-Asturlabi, made astrolabes in Aleppo about the year 950. In 1259, the Maragha observatory was built in what is now Iran, and its astronomers found new ways to use circles to match the planets. About 1370, Mahendra Suri wrote the Yantraraja, the first surviving Sanskrit book on the astrolabe, at the court of Firuz Shah Tughlaq in Delhi. These astronomers made many of the exact tables that Europeans later used.
examples: An astrolabe could tell the time, the direction of Mecca and the height of a star, all on one brass disc.
Ulugh Beg's catalogue of more than 1,000 stars, made in Samarkand about 1437, was the best for generations.
Many star names in use today, such as Aldebaran, come from Arabic.
explanations.art: A brass astrolabe held by a woman at a workbench in Aleppo, with a window showing a night sky.
explanations.context: This card is about the astronomers and instrument makers of the lands between India and Europe.

explanations.concept: What the stars are made of
explanations.definition: In 1925, Cecilia Payne showed that stars are made mostly of hydrogen and helium. This overturned the old belief that stars are made of the same stuff as the Earth.
explanations.description: Starlight can be split into a rainbow with dark lines. Each kind of atom leaves its own pattern of lines. In 1920, the Indian physicist Meghnad Saha worked out how the heat of a star changes the lines that atoms make. Using his equation, Cecilia Payne, a young astronomer at Harvard, studied the lines in the light of many stars in 1925. She found that stars are mostly hydrogen, with some helium, and only a small share of the heavier elements. The senior astronomers did not believe her at first. The senior astronomer Henry Norris Russell told her it was impossible, and she added a line saying so. Four years later, another astronomer confirmed her result, and she was proved right. She later became a professor at Harvard, the first woman to lead a department there.
examples: The Sun is about three quarters hydrogen by mass and one quarter helium.
The same method of splitting light shows what is in galaxies we cannot visit.
Meghnad Saha was born in what is now Bangladesh, and he later became a professor in Kolkata.
explanations.art: A rainbow strip of starlight with dark lines, a young woman at a desk with a notebook and a drawing of the Sun made of hydrogen.
explanations.context: This card is about how scientists learned what stars are made of, and the woman who found it.

explanations.concept: Did old stone circles watch the sky?
explanations.description: In many places, from India to Britain to Egypt, people raised stones and mounds in lines or circles. Some line up with the Sun at the solstice. Some historians think these sites were built to follow the sky. Others say the lines could be an accident, or that the sites had other uses. There is no written record for most of them.
examples: At Stonehenge in England, the Sun rises close to one of the stone lines on the longest day of the year.
At Nabta Playa in southern Egypt, an old stone circle may point to the summer solstice sunrise.

perspectives.explanation: The sunrise lines at Stonehenge are too exact to be luck. The builders knew where the Sun rises at midsummer and midwinter.
With so many stones, some are bound to line up with something. Without writing, we cannot be sure the builders cared about the Sun.
The sites probably did several jobs. They were places for meeting, burying and watching the sky.

explanations.art: A ring of tall stones at dawn with the Sun rising between two of them.
explanations.context: This card is about an open argument: did people who left no writing watch the sky with their stones?

explanations.concept: Did ideas from the Islamic world reach Copernicus?
explanations.description: Some of the small circles that Copernicus used to match the planets look the same as ones invented by astronomers at Maragha and Damascus 200 years earlier, such as Nasir al-Din al-Tusi and Ibn al-Shatir, long before his time. Historians think it is likely that Copernicus or someone close to him learned of them, but nobody has found the book or the person that carried them. Many see this as one clear case of ideas travelling across lands.
examples: The 'Tusi couple' is a way of making straight-line motion from two circles, and it appears again in Copernicus.
Greek books on astronomy were translated into Arabic in Baghdad, and later back into Latin in Spain.

perspectives.explanation: The likeness is too close to be an accident. Some copy of the ideas must have travelled from the East to Europe.
Different astronomers can find the same trick to solve the same problem. We should not claim a link until we find the road it took.

explanations.art: A map with arrows from Maragha and Damascus to Krakow, and a question mark on the road between them.
explanations.context: This card is about an idea scientists are still working out: how astronomy travelled between lands.

agreed.text: The Earth spins once every day, and it goes round the Sun once every year.
agreed.evidence: Foucault's pendulum, the parallax of stars, the yearly shift of starlight, and photographs from spacecraft all show it.

agreed.text: A steady movement cannot be felt. Only changes in movement, such as starting or stopping, are felt.
agreed.evidence: Passengers in smooth trains and aeroplanes, and experiments in closed cabins, all find that nothing inside shows steady movement.

agreed.text: Planets move on ellipses with the Sun at one focus, and they move fastest when closest to the Sun.
agreed.evidence: Kepler found it from Tycho's readings, and every spacecraft sent to a planet has been aimed using it.

agreed.text: Venus shows phases and changes size, because it goes round the Sun and not round the Earth.
agreed.evidence: Anyone with a small telescope can watch Venus change shape over several months.

agreed.text: Jupiter has moons that go round Jupiter, so not everything in the sky goes round the Earth.
agreed.evidence: The four large moons change place from night to night and can be seen with a pair of binoculars.

agreed.text: Stars are made mostly of hydrogen and helium.
agreed.evidence: The lines in starlight, studied since 1925 in thousands of stars, show the same result.

agreed.text: A longer, steadier instrument gives readings that agree more closely.
agreed.evidence: Astronomers from Tycho to Jai Singh built bigger fixed instruments for this reason, and your own quadrant readings show the same.

challenging.claim: The Sun goes round the Earth, because we can see it rise and set.
challenging.who: Nearly everyone, for thousands of years
challenging.for: The Sun clearly moves across the sky, and the ground feels still.
challenging.against: A steady turn cannot be felt, and from a turning Earth the Sun would look exactly the same. Foucault's pendulum, the parallax of stars and photographs from space show that the Earth turns.
challenging.context: This card is about the oldest idea in astronomy: that the Sun goes round us.

challenging.claim: Nobody before Copernicus thought that the Earth moved.
challenging.for: Copernicus's book in 1543 is the one people remember.
challenging.against: Aristarchus of Samos in Greece, about 250 BCE, said that the Earth goes round the Sun. Aryabhata in India wrote in 499 that the Earth spins. Nilakantha in Kerala put the planets in orbit round the Sun about 1500.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that Copernicus was the first to have a moving Earth.

challenging.claim: Copernicus's Sun-centred model was more accurate than Ptolemy's from the start.
challenging.for: It is simpler to say the planets go round the Sun.
challenging.against: Copernicus still used circles and small extra circles. His tables were no more accurate than Ptolemy's. The Sun-centred picture won because Kepler, Galileo and Newton gave it better maths and better evidence.
challenging.context: This card is about whether the Sun-centred model was better at first.

challenging.claim: Galileo's telescope proved that the Earth goes round the Sun.
challenging.for: Galileo's discoveries of Jupiter's moons and the phases of Venus fitted the Sun-centred view.
challenging.against: Tycho's middle model also fitted the phases of Venus, with the Sun going round the Earth and the planets going round the Sun. The telescope showed that Ptolemy's model was wrong, but it did not prove that the Earth moves. That took the proofs of the 1700s and 1800s.
challenging.context: This card is about what Galileo's telescope did and did not prove.

challenging.claim: Summer is hot because the Earth is nearer to the Sun.
challenging.for: A fire is hotter when you are closer to it.
challenging.against: The Earth is closest to the Sun in early January, in the middle of the northern winter. Summer comes from the tilt of the Earth's axis, which makes the Sun climb higher and the days longer.
challenging.context: This card is about a common mix-up between the Earth's path and the seasons.

challenging.claim: The Earth goes round the Sun on a very long, stretched oval.
challenging.for: Kepler said that planets move on ellipses, and diagrams usually draw them stretched to show the idea.
challenging.against: The Earth's path is very close to a circle. If you drew it 20 centimetres wide, it would differ from a circle by less than a millimetre. The drawings in books are stretched on purpose.
challenging.context: This card is about how oval the Earth's path really is.

big_questions.q: In the chair test, you could not tell by feel whether you or the room was turning. So how do we know it is the Earth that turns?
big_questions.hint: Think about the pendulum, the stars and what a spacecraft sees.

big_questions.q: Tycho's readings were only 8 arcminutes away from a circle, and Kepler threw the circle away. When is a small difference worth believing?
big_questions.hint: Think about how sure Kepler was of Tycho's readings, and why that mattered.

big_questions.q: Ptolemy's circles gave good tables for over 1,400 years, and the model was wrong. Does a model have to be true to be useful?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the tables were used for, and what they could not explain.

big_questions.q: Every place has its own noon, but a clock gives one time for the whole country. Which is the real time?
big_questions.hint: Think about what each one is for, and who needs which.

big_questions.q: Aryabhata wrote that the Earth spins in 499, but most people went on thinking the sky turns. Why do good ideas sometimes take hundreds of years to spread?
big_questions.hint: Think about what a person would have needed to see to be sure, and who could check.

big_questions.q: If you lived on Venus, what would you say moves, and what would you say stands still?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you could see from there, and what you could not feel.

big_questions.q: Cecilia Payne found that stars are mostly hydrogen, and was told she was wrong. Why might the same evidence be believed from one person and doubted from another?
big_questions.hint: Think about who gets listened to, and what a careful scientist should do instead.

big_questions.q: A huge stone sundial and a hand-sized one both tell the time. What does the huge one give that the small one cannot?

story.title: The Blurred Edge of the Shadow
story.note: Ishani, her grandmother, Dev, the guide and the visit are made up. The Jantar Mantar in Jaipur is real, and so is the great stone sundial, called the Samrat Yantra. India's clock time is set by the Sun at 82.5 degrees east. In mid-April the Sun reaches its highest point at Jaipur about 27 minutes after 12 o'clock Indian Standard Time.
text: It was a hot April day in Jaipur, and Ishani was nine years old and far from home. She had come from Madurai by train with her grandmother, Ammamma, and her cousin Dev, who was six. Ammamma had a friend in Jaipur and she wanted to see the old observatory.
"It looks like a place where giants left their stairs," said Dev.
He was nearly right. The Jantar Mantar was full of huge stone shapes. There were curved bowls, tall walls and flights of steps that went up and ended in the air. Ishani opened her notebook.
A guide in a green sari came up to them. "I am Sarika Madam," she said. "Raja Sawai Jai Singh built all this nearly 300 years ago. He wanted to measure the sky better than anyone had before."

She led them to the tallest thing in the garden, a stone stairway rising to a point as high as a house with eight floors. Its top edge was a sharp slope. On both sides, a curved stone track was marked in lines.
"This is the Samrat Yantra," said Sarika Madam. "It is a clock. The sloping edge makes a shadow, and the shadow falls on the curved scales."
"Why is it tilted?" asked Ishani. "Why not straight up?"

"Good question. The tilt is exactly the angle of Jaipur's latitude, about 27 degrees. That points the stairway's edge at the Pole Star. And then something nice happens: the shadow turns by exactly the same amount every hour, 15 degrees. The scale can be marked evenly."
Ishani looked at the scale. The shadow of the top edge lay across the stone, a dark band. She frowned and went closer. Then she crouched.
"Madam, the edge is not sharp," she said. "It is blurred. It is dark in the middle and then it fades. Someone has smudged it."
Dev peered at it. "Maybe a pigeon sat on the stone."
Sarika Madam laughed. "No pigeon. Everyone notices it, if they look carefully. Think. Is the Sun a tiny dot, or a round disc?"
"A disc," said Ishani slowly. "A big round ball. It is just far away."

"Every point on that disc makes its own shadow. They overlap in the middle and slide apart at the edges. That is why the edge fades. The dial is huge so that each minute is spread over a long distance, and you can read the middle of the blur very exactly. The shadow creeps about six centimetres a minute."
They watched the dark band crawl across the scale. Ammamma looked at her phone. It said 12:27.
At that moment, the middle of the shadow touched the line marked noon.
"Oh," said Ishani. "The dial says noon, and the phone says twenty-seven minutes past twelve. One of them is wrong."
"Which?" asked Sarika Madam, with a twinkle.
Ishani looked from one to the other. The phone was a famous machine. The stone had been here for nearly 300 years, and was as big as a house. She did not know which to trust.

"The phone shows Indian Standard Time," the guide said. "The whole country keeps one time, set by the Sun at a place far to the east, near Mirzapur. But the Sun does not reach every place at once. The Earth turns, and the Sun gets to the east first and the west later. In Jaipur, the Sun is at its highest about 27 minutes after it was highest at Mirzapur. This dial shows Jaipur's own noon. It is not wrong. It is telling you the time of this place."
Ammamma took out her phone again. "Let me ask my sister in Kolkata." She called, and put the call on loudspeaker.
"Noon?" said her sister. "We had it nearly an hour ago. The Sun is already well past the top."
Dev's mouth fell open. "But it is the same day! How can it be noon here and not there?"

Ishani had stopped writing. She looked up at the Sun, and then, very slowly, she looked at the stone. The stone had not moved. It had never moved. The shadow crept only because the Sun was moving, or because something else was.
"The Sun is not going round us," she said quietly. "We are going round under it. Kolkata is just further ahead on the same big turn."
"Now you are thinking like Jai Singh," said Sarika Madam.
That night, in the guest room, Ishani wrote in her notebook: The dial stays still. The Earth turns under the Sun. Every place has its own noon, and the clock is the one we agree to share.
She stopped. She added one more line. And the edge of a shadow is blurry, because the Sun is big.
story.epiphany: For the parent: the Earth turns steadily towards the east, so the Sun reaches the east of a country before the west. Each place has its own local noon. Indian Standard Time is one agreed clock for the whole country, set by the Sun at 82.5 degrees east. A dial tilted at the latitude of its city and aligned north shows local Sun time. In Jaipur, in mid-April, that is about 27 minutes after the phone's 12 o'clock. The shadow edge is blurred because the Sun is a disc, not a point.
ask: Why is the Samrat Yantra tilted at the angle of Jaipur's latitude?
Why was the edge of the shadow blurred, and where do you read the time on a blurred edge?
Why did the dial say noon when the phone said twenty-seven minutes past twelve?
Why was it already past noon in Kolkata when it was noon in Jaipur?
Ishani said that the stone had never moved. What did she mean the Sun and the Earth were doing?

roots.context: We sat in a spinning chair, lit a ball like Venus, measured angles and drew planet paths. Now we ask what the long argument about the Sun and the Earth teaches about seeing and knowing.

deep_truth.truth: With your eyes shut, a steady turn of the chair was hard to feel. With your eyes open, the room seemed to turn instead. A steady movement is seen only against something else. The Earth turns steadily, so the Sun seems to circle us while we sit still.
deep_truth.habit: We take what we see for what is happening. The Sun rises, so we say it moves. But a sight tells us how things move compared with us, and it cannot tell us which of the two is moving.
deep_truth.evidence: In The Spinning Chair, the turns that were steady were the hardest to feel, and starting and stopping were the easiest. In Galileo's Venus, the same lamp and ball gave very different views from different places. If your own results differ, write them down as they are.

three.who_am_i: You are standing on a ball that spins at about 1,600 kilometres an hour and circles the Sun at about 30 kilometres a second. You feel none of it.
three.what_is_life: Living bodies feel changes: a start, a stop, a bump. A body can get used to a steady movement so completely that it is no longer noticed.
three.what_is_this_world: Motion is always motion compared with something else. The Sun is still in the Earth's story and moving in the Milky Way's story.

roots.thread: The Sun going round us and the Earth turning under the Sun are the same sight from the ground. Aryabhata saw this in 499, with the picture of a boat. To tell the two stories apart, people needed more than looking. They needed a pendulum, a star's tiny shift and a telescope looking at Venus. Even then, the answer was only found by comparing: one view against another. What we know about the sky comes from looking from many places and seeing what stays the same.

teachings.teaching: Aryabhata wrote that a person in a boat moving forward sees still things on the bank moving backwards. In the same way, he wrote, people on the Earth see the still stars moving westwards.
teachings.link: The picture of the boat is the same as the spinning chair. A steady movement makes the world outside seem to move the other way.

teachings.teaching: The verse speaks of the One as moving and not moving, as far and as near, as inside everything and outside everything.
teachings.link: Whether the Sun moves or the Earth moves depends on where you stand. A thing can be said to move and not to move at the same time, depending on what you compare it with.

science.text: All steady motion is only motion compared with something else. No experiment inside a smoothly moving cabin can tell it from standing still.
Whether this means that 'standing still' has no meaning at all is a question that scientists and philosophers still talk about.

other_view.view: Saying the Earth goes round the Sun or the Sun goes round the Earth are both fine ways to describe the same motion. The Sun-centred one is simply much easier to calculate with, which is why we use it to send spacecraft. It is a choice of the easiest description, and not a discovery about who is 'really' still.

practice.title: Watch the Earth turn
practice.say: Find a patch of sunlight on the floor and mark its edge with a piece of tape. Sit still and breathe in slowly. Breathe out slowly. Watch the edge of the light for three minutes. It creeps along the floor. The Sun is not rushing. You are turning slowly under it, on the Earth. Take one more slow breath, and look at the tape again.
practice.kid: Mark the edge of a sunny patch with tape. Sit still. Breathe slowly. Watch the edge creep. You are the one turning.

ask: If you could not feel the Earth turn and could not see the Sun, how would you know it was turning?
Aryabhata's boat, Galileo's ship and your chair all say the same thing. Why might different people find the same idea in different places?
When someone says they are sure, what could you do to check whether it is the world that moves or only their point of view?
roots.art: A child on a swivel chair with eyes closed in a room, and across the window a patch of sunlight with a tape mark at its edge and a faint picture of the Earth turning outside.

games.title: Claim and Proof: a pairs game of what people said and how they showed it
games.context: This is a memory game. Each pair is a claim about the sky and the evidence that showed it. When you find a pair, say in your own words why the evidence backs up the claim.

setup.art: Twenty cards face down in four rows on a mat, with two turned up: a claim card and its proof card.
setup.caption: 1. Lay the cards face down. Turn over two.

setup.art: A child holding a matched pair and explaining it to a parent.
setup.caption: 2. A match? Say why the proof fits the claim.

printables.title: 20 cards: 10 claims and 10 proofs to cut out
items: CLAIM: The Earth is round.
PROOF: The Earth's shadow on the Moon in an eclipse is always round, and ships disappear hull first.
CLAIM: Venus goes round the Sun.
PROOF: Through a telescope in 1610, Venus changed from a big thin crescent to a small, nearly full disc.
CLAIM: Jupiter has moons that go round it.
PROOF: Four small lights near Jupiter changed places night after night and stayed with the planet.
CLAIM: A planet moves on an ellipse, not on a circle.
PROOF: Tycho's readings of Mars differ from the best circle by 8 arcminutes, which is too much to be a mistake.
CLAIM: The Earth spins.
PROOF: A long pendulum slowly changes the direction of its swing over the floor, while the Earth turns under it.
CLAIM: The stars are very far away.
PROOF: Bessel found a star's tiny shift in 1838. The shift was so small that the star had to be many light-years away.
CLAIM: A bigger instrument can be read more finely.
PROOF: On a stone dial 27 metres tall, a minute of time is spread over about six centimetres of scale.
CLAIM: Stars are mostly hydrogen and helium.
PROOF: The dark lines in starlight, read by Cecilia Payne in 1925, match those of hydrogen and helium.
CLAIM: The Earth's size can be measured without leaving the ground.
PROOF: Al-Biruni climbed a mountain and measured how far the horizon dips below level.
CLAIM: A steady movement cannot be felt.
PROOF: With your eyes shut, you could tell the chair was turning only when it started or stopped.

printables.title: Score sheet
items: Player name
Pairs kept
Reasons said in your own words

rules: Shuffle all 20 cards and lay them face down in rows. Each pair is one CLAIM card and the PROOF card that goes with it.
On your turn, turn over two cards.
If they are a claim and its proof, read both aloud. Then say in your own words why the proof backs up the claim. If you can, you keep the pair.
If you cannot say why, turn both cards back. Everyone has now seen where they are.
If they are not a pair, turn them back face down. The next player has a turn.
When all pairs are found, the player with the most pairs wins. If two players have the same number, they win together.
Playing alone, count the number of turns you take and try to beat it next time.

flow.do: Cut out the 20 cards. Read all the pairs together once, face up. Then shuffle them and lay them face down.
flow.say: Each pair is a claim about the sky and the proof for it. Let's read them all first. Then we hide them.
flow.kid: Read all the cards first. Then turn them face down.
flow.context: This is the first step of Claim and Proof, a memory game about how people showed things about the sky.
flow.parent: Scissors are for a grown-up or an older child. The game suits one to four players. Playing alone, lay the cards out and count your turns.

flow.do: Take turns turning over two cards. Keep a pair only if the player can say why the proof backs up the claim.
flow.say: You found a pair. Now tell me in your own words, how does this proof show this claim?
flow.kid: Turn over two cards. A match? Say why the proof fits.
flow.parent: Help with the harder ones. A good reason for the Tycho pair: his readings were so careful that a gap of 8 arcminutes had to be real.

check.q: Why does a long pendulum change its swing direction over the floor?
options: The floor is turning under it, because the Earth spins
check.why: A pendulum keeps swinging in the same direction in space. The Earth turns under it, so the swing seems to turn over the floor.

flow.do: Count the pairs. Ask one question.
flow.say: Which proof was the hardest to believe? What would you want to check yourself?
flow.kid: Which proof surprised you most? Why?

games.title: Courtroom of the Sky: argue like an astronomer of the past
games.context: This is a role-play game. Players are astronomers from history. A judge reads a question about the sky, and each astronomer answers using only what they knew in their own time.

setup.art: A table with a pile of question cards, eight role cards laid out face up, and a child as the judge holding a pebble.
setup.caption: 1. The judge reads a question. The witnesses take role cards.

setup.art: A child in a paper hat speaking while others listen, and the judge handing a pebble to the best speaker.
setup.caption: 2. Answer in character. The judge gives a pebble to the best argument.

printables.title: 8 role cards: a person on the front, what they could say on the back

items.b: The Earth is still at the centre. Planets loop because they ride small circles on big circles. My tables work.
The Earth spins, and the stars only seem to move west, as the bank seems to move backwards from a boat. Eclipses are shadows.
I doubt the Earth moves. Birds that fly up from a tree would not find their tree again. Things would be left behind.
The planets go round the Sun, and the Sun goes round the Earth. This explains their looping paths neatly.
The Sun is at the centre. The Earth is a planet that spins and goes round the Sun. I still use circles and small circles.
I have measured planets to one arcminute for years. The planets go round the Sun and the Sun goes round the Earth. I cannot feel the Earth move.
Mars moves on an ellipse. Tycho's readings are never wrong by 8 arcminutes, so I gave up the circle. A planet moves faster when it is closer to the Sun.
My telescope shows moons round Jupiter, the phases of Venus, mountains on the Moon and countless stars. Ptolemy's Venus is wrong.

printables.title: 10 question cards: a question on the front, a good answer on the back

items.f: Why does Mars sometimes seem to go backwards?
items.b: A good answer says either that Mars rides a small circle, or that the faster Earth overtakes it, as a car passes a lorry.
A good answer gives the evidence of that person's time and says what would still be missing.

items.f: What shape is the path of a planet?
items.b: Circles for the earlier people. An ellipse for Kepler, because Tycho's readings would not fit a circle.

items.f: Does Venus ever look nearly full?
items.b: Not in Ptolemy's model. It does in a telescope, which means that Venus goes round the Sun.

items.f: Why can nobody feel the Earth turning?
items.b: A steady movement cannot be felt, only changes. Galileo's ship and Aryabhata's boat both show this.

items.f: Should you trust a careful measurement that does not fit a beautiful idea?
items.b: Kepler did. A good answer explains why very careful readings are worth more than a pleasing shape.

items.f: What can a telescope show that eyes cannot?
items.b: Moons of Jupiter, the phases of Venus, craters on the Moon and many fainter stars.

items.f: Why would anyone build a stone observatory as big as a house?
items.b: A bigger instrument has a bigger scale and can be read more finely. Stone does not bend like thin brass.

items.f: How could you find out how far away a star is?
items.b: By looking at it from two places far apart, such as two sides of the Earth's orbit, and measuring its tiny shift.

items.f: If the Earth moves, why do birds find their nests?
items.b: The air and the birds move along with the Earth, as a fly in a smooth moving train moves with the train.

printables.title: A handful of pebbles, buttons or paper counters for the judge to hand out
items: Cut out 12 small paper circles to use as points.

rules: One player is the judge. Everyone else takes a role card. With only two or three players, one player may take two roles.
The judge reads one question card aloud, without showing the back.
Each astronomer gets 20 seconds to answer in character, using only what their card says they knew in their own time.
The judge decides whose answer used the best evidence, and gives that player a point.
The judge reads the back of the question card. Everyone talks about what the best answer left out.
After three questions, the judge swaps with another player. After ten questions, the player with the most points wins.

Playing with just a parent, take turns being the judge and a witness, and swap roles after each question. With just one child and a parent, the child draws two role cards and answers each question twice, once as each person, and the parent as judge picks the better answer.

flow.do: Cut out the cards. Choose a judge. Hand out the role cards. Each player reads their card quietly.
flow.say: You are an astronomer from the past. Read your card. You know only what is written on the back.
flow.kid: Take a role card. Read it. You know only what it says.
flow.context: This is the first step of Courtroom of the Sky, a role-play about what astronomers of the past could say.

flow.do: Play the first question cards. The judge hands out points and reads the backs. After the third question, ask the question below.
flow.say: Judge, read the question. Astronomers, answer in character. Now judge, whose argument used the best evidence?
flow.kid: The judge reads. Answer as your person would. The judge picks the best.

ask.q: Which astronomer's answer sounded most convincing at the time?
good: The one who had the most careful readings.
The one who used a telescope.
It depends what they could see in their own time.

flow.parent: Remind players that each person could only use the evidence of their own time, and could not use anything found later.
flow.context: In this step you play the first questions and learn how the judge scores.

flow.do: Count the points and talk about which person you liked best.
flow.say: Who had the best argument for their time? Who was right but could not prove it yet?
flow.kid: Who was right but could not prove it yet?

check.q: In 499, Aryabhata said that the Earth spins, but he could not prove it. Was he right?
options: Yes, he was right, though the proof came much later
No, because he had no proof
No, because the Earth does not spin
check.why: An idea can be right before there is evidence for it. Evidence from pendulums, stars and spacecraft came centuries later, and agreed with him.

experiments.title: The Spinning Chair: can you feel a steady turn?
experiments.question: You sit in a swivel chair that a grown-up turns slowly and smoothly. With your eyes shut, can you tell whether the chair is turning or still? And with your eyes open, who seems to be turning, you or the room?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. With your eyes shut, will you be able to feel a slow, steady turn? Will you feel it start or stop? With your eyes open, who will seem to turn, you or the room? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same chair and the same turning speed every time, about one full turn in ten seconds. The grown-up decides in secret, by drawing slips, which rounds are turning and which are still. The child wears a scarf over the eyes and hums a tune, so that sounds give nothing away. Play six rounds. Only the secret order changes.

materials.item: a swivel chair or an office chair that turns smoothly and does not squeak, or a stool on a thick cloth on a smooth floor that a grown-up can turn by the legs
a scarf or a soft cloth, to cover the eyes
6 small slips of paper, three marked TURN and three marked STILL, folded and mixed in a bowl (for 2 to 4 children, make a fresh set of 4 for each child, two TURN and two STILL)
5 sheets of paper marked A to E, stuck on the walls of the room at the child's eye height
a phone timer or a clock with a seconds hand
a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: Turn the chair slowly, never faster than one turn in ten seconds. Stop at once if the child feels dizzy or sick, and let her rest for five minutes. Keep the floor around the chair clear of furniture and sharp corners. A grown-up holds the chair steady when the child gets on and off. Children who get dizzy easily, or have ear problems, should skip this test.

schedule.what: Try the chair with the eyes open, then with the eyes shut for six rounds. Score the answers. Then think about the Earth, which turns steadily too.

experiments.record: Fill in the table and count the right answers. Under it, write one sentence about what you could feel and what you could not.

flow.do: Show your child the chair, the scarf and the slips. Ask for a guess about the eyes-shut test and the eyes-open test, and a reason. Write the guess.
flow.say: You will sit in this chair. With your eyes shut, can you tell if it turns slowly and steadily? With your eyes open, who seems to be turning? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Eyes shut, can you feel a slow turn? Eyes open, who seems to turn?

ask.q: Why do you think you will, or will not, feel it?
good: You can feel your body being pulled round.
The turn is too slow and smooth to feel.
It is hard to tell without seeing.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children are sure that they will feel the turn. Write down the guess.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Spinning Chair test. You guess before you test.

flow.do: With the eyes open, turn the chair very slowly. Ask the child which sheet of paper is straight ahead as it passes. Then ask: is the room turning, or is the chair? Stop the chair gently.
flow.say: I will turn the chair very slowly. Call out the letter on the wall that is straight in front of you. Is the room turning round you, or are you turning round the room?
flow.kid: Eyes open. Call out the letter in front of you. Who is turning?
flow.parent: The child can tell by looking that the room seems to turn the other way. This is the picture in Aryabhata's boat: when you move, the world seems to move backwards. Keep the turning slow and smooth.
flow.context: In this step you try the chair with your eyes open, and see how the room seems to move.

flow.do: Cover the eyes with the scarf. Draw a slip in secret. On a TURN slip, start the chair very gently and build up to one turn in ten seconds. On a STILL slip, touch the chair lightly and do nothing. After 20 seconds, ask: turning or still? Write down the answer. Do six rounds.
flow.say: Eyes shut and hum a tune. In a moment I will either turn you slowly or keep you still. After a little while, tell me: turning or still?
flow.kid: Eyes shut. Hum a tune. After a while say: turning or still?
flow.parent: Start each TURN round very gently, so that the push is hard to feel, and keep the turn steady. In a STILL round, make the same small touch and noises. If the child is right six times, ask which clue she used, such as a breeze, a creak or a touch. Chance alone gives about three right out of six. Your own results decide what you write. One child with a parent: the parent turns the chair and draws the slips, and the child plays all six rounds. With 2 to 4 children: one is the turner, one is the scorer, and each child in the chair plays four rounds, so the whole group takes about 15 minutes. Add up all the right answers and compare with half of all rounds, which is what guessing gives. Many children score near chance and a few do better, because a gentle start can sometimes be felt. Both results are honest. Write down what you got.

check.q: Why does the grown-up draw the slips in secret and make a small touch on every round?
options: So that the child cannot guess from any clue except the turning itself
To make the game last longer
So the chair does not wear out
check.why: A fair test changes one thing, which here is whether the chair turns. If the child could hear or feel something else that gave the answer away, you would not be testing the turning.

flow.context: In this step you play six rounds with the eyes shut, and score each answer.

flow.do: Count the right answers. Then do one last round: turn the chair steadily, with the eyes shut, and stop it suddenly. Ask what the child felt.
flow.say: Let's count how many you got right. Chance would give about three. Now one last try. I will turn you and then stop the chair quite suddenly. What do you feel?
flow.kid: Count your right answers. Then feel what happens when the chair stops.
flow.parent: Most children feel the sudden stop clearly, as a lean or a wobble inside the body. The turn itself is much harder to feel once it is steady. Stop the chair gently, with your hand on its back, so nobody tips.

check.q: When the chair stopped suddenly with your eyes shut, what did you feel?
options: A lean or a push, because stopping is a change of movement
check.why: Our bodies feel changes in movement, such as starts, stops and turns. A steady movement is not felt. The sudden stop was a big change, so it was easy to feel.

flow.do: Ask for what I think, what I saw and why. Then ask about the Earth.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you notice that shows it? And why? The Earth turns steadily once a day. Would you feel it?
flow.kid: Say what I think, what I saw and why. Would you feel the Earth turn?
flow.parent: This is claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer: what I think: a slow steady turn is hard or impossible to feel. What I saw: for example, I got three or four of six right, which is about what chance gives, but I felt the sudden stop. If you got five or six right, say which clue you used. Why: our bodies sense changes in movement, and a steady movement has no change to sense. The Earth turns steadily, and never starts or stops, so we feel nothing. With eyes open, the room seemed to turn the other way, as the bank does from a boat. That is why the Sun seems to move across the sky when it is we who are turning.

check.q: The Earth turns once every 24 hours without stopping. Why can we not feel it?
options: It turns steadily, and we feel only changes in movement
It turns too fast to feel
We are too small to feel it
check.why: The Earth never speeds up or slows down in a way we can feel. A steady turn, like the steady chair, gives the body nothing to sense. At Chennai the ground moves at about 1,630 kilometres an hour, and we feel none of it.

experiments.context: In this experiment you sit in a spinning chair with your eyes shut and try to feel a slow, steady turn. It shows why nobody could feel the Earth turn, and why the Sun seems to go round us.

experiments.title: Galileo's Venus: can Venus look full if it stays between us and the Sun?
experiments.question: In Ptolemy's Earth-centred model, Venus rides a small circle between the Earth and the Sun. In a Sun-centred model, Venus goes round the Sun. Which model can make Venus look nearly full, as Galileo saw it in 1610?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which phases of Venus can each model make? Will the ball look bigger when it is a thin crescent or when it is nearly full? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same lamp, the same ball and the same viewing spot for both models, in a dark room. Only the path of the ball changes: a small circle between you and the lamp for the Earth-centred model, and a big circle round the lamp for the Sun-centred model. Look at the ball from the same height at every stop.
results_table: How much of the ball looks lit? (none, thin, half, nearly all)
Does the ball look small or big?

materials.item: a lamp with a bare LED bulb and no shade, such as a table lamp with its shade taken off or an LED emergency lantern, standing on a stool or a stack of books at the height of a seated child's eyes. A torch will not do, because it lights only one side and the ball behind it would stay dark
a white ball, about 4 centimetres across, such as a table-tennis ball, a white lime or a ball of white paper, stuck on the end of a pencil with a blob of clay
a chair, for the viewer, 2 metres from the lamp
2 pieces of string, one 40 centimetres long and one 70 centimetres long
masking tape, to mark the floor
a dark room in the evening, with the curtains shut
paper and pencil

experiments.safety: Use an LED bulb or torch, which stays cool. Never use a hot halogen lamp. Do not stare into the bright bulb. A grown-up sets up the lamp so that the wire is out of the way and nobody trips.

schedule.what: Set up the lamp, the chair and the strings. Move the ball around the Earth-centred path and then around the Sun-centred path. Record the shapes and sizes. Compare with what Galileo saw.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Draw the ball as you saw it at each stop, with the lit part shaded white.

flow.do: Show your child the lamp, the ball and the strings. Say that the lamp is the Sun and the ball is Venus. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: The lamp is the Sun and the ball is Venus. In one model, Venus stays between us and the Sun. In the other, it goes right round the Sun. Which one can make Venus look full? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Lamp is the Sun. Ball is Venus. Which model can make it look full? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think that model will, or will not, make a full Venus?
good: If it stays in front of the lamp, we only see its dark side.
If it goes behind the lamp, we see the lit side.
I am not sure. Let's try.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. A lit ball always has half lit, facing the lamp. What we see depends on where we stand.
flow.context: This is the first step of Galileo's Venus. You guess before you test.

flow.do: Put the lamp at one end of the room and the viewer's chair 2 metres away. Turn off all other lights. Tape a small cross on the floor halfway between the chair and the lamp. Tie the 40 centimetre string to a pencil and hold it at the cross. Tie the 70 centimetre string to the lamp's stand.
flow.say: The chair is the Earth. The lamp is the Sun. The cross halfway is the middle of Ptolemy's small circle. The long string will be the big circle round the Sun.
flow.kid: Chair is Earth. Lamp is Sun. Mark a cross halfway between them.
flow.parent: The ball must be at the same height as the lamp, so hold it at the level of the bulb. Sit in the chair with your eyes at the ball's height if you can. Keep your head still while you look. Roles for one child with a parent: the parent walks the ball and the child looks and records. For 2 to 4 children: one sits in the chair and looks, one walks the ball, one keeps the lamp steady and calls the stop, and one records. Swap jobs after each model so that everyone looks at least once. If the ball looks evenly lit at every stop, light is leaking in. Shut the curtains and wait for full dark, or turn off every other light.
flow.context: In this step you set up the lamp, the chair and the strings for the two models.

flow.do: Earth-centred model: hold the ball at the end of the 40 centimetre string, keeping the string tight round the cross. Stop at four places: nearest the chair, to the left, farthest from the chair, and to the right. At each stop, look and record what you see.
flow.say: In this model Venus stays on a small circle between you and the Sun. Stop at the four places. At each one, how much of the ball is lit? Does it ever look full?
flow.kid: Move the ball round the small circle. Stop four times. How much is lit?
flow.parent: Expected: the ball looks like a thin crescent at the left and right stops, and almost dark at the near and far stops, where its lit side faces away from you. It never looks more than a thin crescent. This is the best Ptolemy's Venus could do.

check.q: In the Earth-centred model, the ball stays between you and the lamp. What phases can it show?
check.why: The lamp always lights the half of the ball that faces the lamp. If the ball stays in front of the lamp, most of what you see is the unlit side. So it can only look like a thin crescent.

flow.do: Sun-centred model: hold the ball at the end of the 70 centimetre string tied to the lamp stand. Walk it all the way round the lamp. Stop at five places. These are nearest the chair, the left side, behind and left of the lamp, behind and right, and the right side. At each stop, record what you see.
flow.say: In this model Venus goes right round the Sun. Walk the ball round and stop at five places. How much is lit? When does it look biggest? When does it look nearly full? How big does it look then?
flow.kid: Walk the ball all the way round the lamp. Stop five times. What do you see?
flow.parent: Expected: nearest the chair, the ball is mostly dark and looks big. At the sides, you see half. Behind the lamp, off to one side so the lamp does not block your view, you see nearly all of the ball lit, and it looks smaller because it is about twice as far (about 2.7 metres, against 1.3 metres nearest the chair). The crescents and the half are easy to see. The nearly full ball is the faint one, so look from a little to the side of the lamp so that the bulb does not dazzle you. This is what Galileo saw.

check.q: When did the ball look nearly full in the Sun-centred model?
options: When it was on the far side of the lamp from you
When it was between you and the lamp
check.why: When the ball is beyond the lamp, the lit half faces you. A ball can be seen almost full only if it can go behind the lamp. That is also why it looks small then, because it is farther away.

flow.do: Ask for what I think, what I saw and why. Then tell the story of Galileo and Venus.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why? Galileo saw Venus nearly full and small in late 1610, and later as a big thin crescent. Which model fits?
flow.kid: Say what I think, what I saw and why. Which model fits Galileo?
flow.parent: This is claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer: what I think: Venus must go round the Sun, and not just stay in front of it. What I saw: in the Earth-centred circle the ball never looked more than a thin crescent. In the Sun-centred circle it looked nearly full when it was far side, and small. Why: a ball can look full only if it can go behind the lamp. Be fair to Tycho: his middle model, where the Sun goes round the Earth and Venus goes round the Sun, also fits. So Galileo showed that Ptolemy's Venus was wrong. He did not yet prove that the Earth moves.

check.q: Galileo saw Venus look nearly full through his telescope. What did that show?
options: Venus can go behind the Sun, so it goes round the Sun
Venus is bigger than the Sun
check.why: A nearly full Venus must be seen from the far side of its path. That means it goes round the Sun, and not just in front of it. Ptolemy's model could not make this happen.

experiments.context: In this experiment you use a lamp and a ball to find which models of Venus can show every phase. It repeats the telescope discovery of Galileo that ended Ptolemy's model of the planets.

experiments.title: Tycho's Quadrant: how precisely can you measure an angle?
experiments.question: A sticker is stuck high up on a wall. If you measure its angle above the horizontal ten times, how much do your readings differ? Do a steadier instrument and a longer sighting tube make the readings agree more closely?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Will your ten readings all be the same, nearly the same, or very different? Will resting the quadrant on a table help? Will a longer straw help? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same sticker, the same standing place and the same quadrant. Take ten readings for each setup. Only the setup changes: first the quadrant held in your hands with a short straw, then the quadrant resting on a table with the short straw, then resting on the table with a long straw. Look away between readings so that you do not remember the last number.

materials.item: a piece of stiff card about 25 centimetres square, from a box
a half-circle protractor, 12 to 15 centimetres across, marked from 0 to 180 degrees
2 drinking straws, one cut to 8 centimetres and one cut to 25 centimetres
30 centimetres of thread and a washer, a nut or a pea-sized blob of clay for a weight
cello tape
a coloured sticker or a dot of coloured paper, stuck on a wall about 1 metre above eye level
a pair of scissors for a grown-up to use, a table, a tape measure, a notebook and a pencil

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the straws if the child is younger than eight. Use a steady table and do not stand on a chair to reach the sticker. Scissors and the cut ends of straws are sharp, so a grown-up does the cutting. Keep the washer or nut away from children under five.

schedule.what: Build the quadrant. Take ten readings in each of three setups. Find the spread of each. Think about what Tycho's huge instruments gave him.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. For each setup, circle the smallest and the biggest reading. Change the spread from degrees to arcminutes by multiplying by 60.

flow.do: Show your child the protractor, the straws and the sticker. Ask for a guess about the readings, and a reason. Write the guess.
flow.say: We will make a quadrant to measure how high the sticker is. If we measure ten times, will we get the same number each time? Will a steadier setup help? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Measure the angle ten times. Will you get the same number? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think your readings will, or will not, be the same?
good: My hand shakes, so they will differ.
If I am careful they will be the same.
A table will hold it still, so they will be closer.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Remind your child that the word precision means how closely repeated readings agree.
flow.context: This is the first step of Tycho's Quadrant. You guess before you build.

flow.do: Tape the protractor's flat edge to the card's edge, with the curved side away from the card. Tape the short straw along the flat edge. Tape the thread at the protractor's centre mark, and tie the weight to its other end so that it hangs freely.
flow.say: The straw is the sight. You look through it at the sticker. The thread hangs straight down, and it crosses the numbers on the scale. That number tells you the angle.
flow.kid: Tape the straw to the flat edge. Tape a hanging thread at the centre mark.
flow.parent: To read the angle: sight the sticker along the straw. Hold the thread against the card with a finger so that it stops swinging. Read the number on the scale. When the straw is level, the thread crosses 90. The angle of the sticker is the difference between the reading and 90, whichever way round. For example, a reading of 63 means 27 degrees.

check.q: When the straw points level, the thread crosses the 90 mark. The thread crosses 63 when you sight the sticker. What is the sticker's angle above level?
check.why: The thread hangs straight down whatever you do. The angle between its 90 mark and where it crosses is how far the straw has tipped from level. 90 take away 63 is 27 degrees.

flow.context: In this step you build the quadrant and learn how to read it.

flow.do: Stand 2 metres from the wall. Hold the quadrant in your hands with the short straw. Sight the sticker, pinch the thread and read the number. Write it down. Look away, then do it nine more times.
flow.say: Hold the quadrant in your hands. Look through the straw at the sticker. Pinch the thread and read. Write it down, look away, and try again. Ten times.
flow.kid: Hold the quadrant. Sight the sticker. Pinch the thread. Read. Ten times.
flow.parent: Stand in the same place every time. Mark the spot with tape. Expect the readings to differ by a few degrees when the quadrant is held in the hands. One child with a parent: the child sights and pinches the thread, and the parent reads and writes the number, or the child does both. For 2 to 4 children: one sights and pinches, one reads, one writes, and each child takes a turn at each job. Compare the spreads of different children too. Everyone should use the same quadrant and the same standing mark.
flow.context: In this step you take ten readings with the quadrant held in your hands.

flow.do: Rest the quadrant on the edge of a table at the same standing place. Use the same short straw. Take ten more readings. Then swap to the long straw and take ten more.
flow.say: Now rest the quadrant on the table edge. Take ten more readings. Then swap to the long straw and take ten more. Are the numbers closer together?
flow.kid: Rest the quadrant on a table. Ten readings. Then the long straw. Ten more.
flow.parent: The table takes away the shaking of the hand, and the long straw makes it easier to aim at a small sticker. Expect the spread to fall, but your own results decide. For the long straw, tape it along the flat edge so that it sticks out past the card, in place of the short one. If the table does not help your readings, write that down as it is. A common cause is a thread that still swings, so pinch it slowly and read it twice.

check.q: Which setup do you expect to have the smallest spread?
options: Resting on a table with the long straw
Held in the hands with the short straw
They will all be the same
check.why: A steady rest and a longer sight both help aim at the same spot every time. So the readings should agree more closely. If your results differ, write them down as they are and ask why.

flow.do: Work out the spread for each setup. Change each spread into arcminutes by multiplying by 60. Ask for what I think, what I saw and why. Then ask about Tycho.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why? Tycho's best readings were good to one arcminute. How does that compare with yours?
flow.kid: Find each spread. Times 60 for arcminutes. How does Tycho compare?
flow.parent: This is claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer: what I think: a steadier, longer instrument gives readings that agree more closely. What I saw: the spread went from, for example, 5 degrees in my hands to 2 degrees on the table and 1 degree with the long straw. Why: shaking and hard aiming cause the readings to scatter, and a table and a long sight reduce both. Then Tycho: 1 degree is 60 arcminutes. If your best spread is 1 degree, Tycho's one arcminute was 60 times more precise. This is why he built huge brass instruments, fixed in place, with finely marked scales. And it is why Kepler could trust a gap of 8 arcminutes. With your quadrant, a gap of 8 arcminutes would have been invisible.

check.q: Your best spread is 1 degree. How many arcminutes is that, and could you have noticed Kepler's gap of 8 arcminutes?
options: 60 arcminutes, and no, the gap is hidden inside the spread
check.why: One degree has 60 arcminutes. A gap of 8 arcminutes is much smaller than the spread of your readings, so you could not see it. Tycho's readings were good to about one arcminute, so 8 arcminutes stood out clearly.

experiments.context: In this experiment you build a simple quadrant and measure the same angle many times. It shows what precision means and why Tycho Brahe built giant, steady instruments.
