activities.title: Kepler's Ellipse: draw a planet's path with string and two pins

materials.item: a piece of thick corrugated cardboard from a carton (two layers taped together) or a thermocol sheet, about 40 centimetres square, so that the pins hold firm
a sheet of plain paper, A3, taped on the card
2 drawing pins or thumb tacks
a loop of strong thread that does not stretch, 24 centimetres round, with a tight knot (a thread that stretches makes the shapes come out wrong)
a sharp pencil and a ruler

activities.safety: Drawing pins are sharp. A grown-up pushes them in and takes them out, and counts them back into the box when the activity is over.

schedule.what: Draw a circle and four ellipses with the pins at different distances. Measure each. Find out what Kepler's Mars would look like.

activities.record: Keep all five drawings on one page, and fill in a table with the pin distance, the width and the height of each shape.

flow.do: Show your child the pins, the loop and the pencil. Ask what shape will appear when the pins are in the same place. Then ask what will happen if you move the pins apart. Write down the guesses.
flow.say: Kepler found that a planet's path is an ellipse. We can draw one with a loop of thread and two pins. What shape will we get if both pins are in the same spot? What if we move them apart?
flow.kid: A loop of thread and two pins. What shape comes if the pins are together? Apart?
flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. A circle is an ellipse with both foci in the same place.
flow.context: This is the first step of the ellipse drawing. You guess before you draw.

flow.do: A grown-up pushes both pins into the card at the same spot, in the middle of the paper. Put the loop round the pins. Put the pencil inside the loop and pull it tight. Slide the pencil all the way round, keeping the thread tight. You draw a circle.
flow.say: Both pins are in the same place. The thread is tight against the pencil. Slide the pencil all the way round. What shape do you get?
flow.kid: Pins together. Pull the thread tight. Slide the pencil all the way round.
flow.parent: Keep the pencil upright and the thread tight at all times. The circle should be 24 centimetres across. If the thread slips off the pins, use a little tape over their heads.
flow.context: In this step you draw the first shape, with both pins in one place.

flow.do: Move the pins 2 centimetres apart, on a line across the middle of the paper. Draw a new shape the same way. Do the same with the pins 4 centimetres apart, and with 8 centimetres apart. Measure the width and the height of each shape.
flow.say: Now the pins are 2 centimetres apart. Draw again. Measure how wide it is and how tall. Is it still a circle? Now try 4 centimetres, and then 8.
flow.kid: Move the pins 2 centimetres apart. Draw again. Measure width and height.
flow.parent: Expected: pins 0 apart gives 24 by 24 centimetres. Pins 2 apart gives about 22 wide and 21.9 tall. Pins 4 apart gives about 20 wide and 19.6 tall. Pins 8 apart gives about 16 wide and 13.9 tall. The first two look the same to the eye. Measure with a ruler across the middle of each shape. Check it with a sum: the width is 24 minus the gap between the pins, for a loop of 24 centimetres. Predict the width before you draw each shape. Your ruler readings will be a little off, by a few millimetres, from the numbers above. One child with a parent: the parent holds the board and measures. For 2 to 4 children: each draws a different gap (0, 2, 4 and 8 centimetres) on a shared board, one at a time, and then the shapes are laid side by side. If the thread bunches or the pencil slips, keep the pencil upright and the thread tight.

check.q: What happens to the shape as the two pins are moved farther apart, with the same loop?
options: It gets flatter and more oval
check.why: The loop stays the same length, so the pencil can reach less far across the line between the pins. The shape stretches along the pin line, and it gets squashed the other way.

flow.do: Look at the shape with the pins 2 centimetres apart. Mark each pin spot with a dot. The pin spots are called foci. Ask which one is the Sun. Then look at how far the Sun is from the middle of the shape.
flow.say: Mars has a path like the shape with pins 2 centimetres apart. It looks like a circle. But the Sun is at one pin, and the pin is 1 centimetre from the middle. That small gap is what Kepler used. What would a circle say about where the Sun is?
flow.kid: Put a dot at each pin. The Sun is at one. How far is it from the middle?
flow.parent: This shape is close to the real path of Mars, whose Sun is off-centre by about a tenth of the path's radius. A circle with the Sun in the middle would be 1 centimetre wrong. Tycho's readings were good enough to notice that.

check.q: The path of Mars looks almost exactly like a circle. How did Kepler know it was an ellipse?
options: Careful readings showed the Sun is off-centre, and that a circle missed by 8 arcminutes
He measured the width of the path with a ruler
He saw it through a telescope
check.why: To the eye, Mars's path is almost a circle. Only careful readings revealed the gap. Kepler trusted Tycho's readings enough to follow the gap, and found the ellipse.

activities.context: In this activity you draw a circle and four ellipses using a loop of thread and two pins. It shows what Kepler found, and how close to a circle the planets' paths really are.

activities.title: A Sundial for Your City: build a small Samrat Yantra

materials.item: a square of stiff card, 15 centimetres by 15 centimetres
a half-circle protractor
a new unsharpened pencil or a thick wooden stick, about 15 centimetres long, for the gnomon
modelling clay and a few books to prop the dial
a phone with a compass and a clock
a sunny windowsill, balcony or terrace
a ruler, a pencil and a notebook

activities.safety: Never look at the Sun. Read the dial only by looking at the shadow on it. Go on a terrace or balcony only with a grown-up.

schedule.what: Look up your latitude, make the dial plate, mark the hour lines and push the stick through the middle.
On a sunny day, prop the dial at your city's tilt, point it north, and compare its shadow with your phone clock at four times.

activities.record: Fill in a table with the phone time and the dial time at four moments, and the difference between them each time.

flow.do: Find your city's latitude. Take away this number from 90 to get the tilt. Chennai is about 13 degrees, so the tilt is 77. Kochi is about 10 and Bengaluru about 13. Hyderabad is about 17, Pune about 18 and Mumbai about 19. Kolkata is about 23, Jaipur about 27 and Delhi about 29.
flow.say: Every sundial must be tilted for its own city. Look up your latitude. Then take it away from 90. That is the tilt of your dial from flat. Why do you think a different city needs a different tilt?
flow.kid: Find your latitude. Take it away from 90. That is your dial's tilt.
flow.parent: The tilt makes the dial plate parallel to the Earth's equator. That way, the Sun's shadow turns evenly, 15 degrees every hour, because the Earth turns 15 degrees every hour. At Jaipur, the tilt of the great stone dial is its latitude, about 27 degrees.
flow.context: This is the first step of the sundial. You find the tilt that your city needs.

flow.do: Mark a dot in the middle of the card. Use the protractor to draw 13 lines from the dot to the edge, 15 degrees apart. Make one line point straight down the page and write 12 on it. Write 11 down to 6 on the right and 1 up to 6 on the left. Then hold the card to a window and trace the lines on the back. Write the same hours on the same lines.
flow.say: Draw the noon line straight down. Then draw a line every 15 degrees. Each one is an hour. Mark both sides of the card, because in some months the Sun lights the back of the dial. The back has the same lines in the same places.
flow.kid: Mark the middle. Draw lines 15 degrees apart. Write the hours on the lines.
flow.parent: The Sun is north of the equator from about March to September. Then the shadow falls on the upper face. From about September to March, it is south of the equator and the shadow falls on the lower face. A card with hours on both faces works all year. The hours run this way when you look at the front with the 12 at the bottom, because morning shadows fall to the west. Tracing through a window makes the back match the front, so that the same hour sits on the same line.
flow.context: In this step you mark the hour lines on both faces of the dial.

flow.do: Push the pencil through the middle dot, straight, so that it sticks out equally on both sides. Prop the card on books and clay so that the card is tilted from flat by your tilt number. Check with the protractor. Turn the dial so that the 12 line points down the slope to the north. The top of the pencil also points north.
flow.say: The pencil is the gnomon. The pencil should point at the Pole Star, which is at the north. The card is tilted so that the pencil points up at the angle of your latitude. Check with the protractor.
flow.kid: Push the stick through the middle. Tilt the card. Point the stick north.
flow.parent: Use a phone compass to find north. In India, magnetic north differs from true north by only a degree or two, which is fine. The pencil must make an angle with the flat ground equal to your latitude. For Chennai, that is 13 degrees. Day 1 stops here. No phone compass? Use the north-south line from the stick-shadow challenge. One child with a parent: the parent holds the compass while the child tilts and checks the angle. For 2 to 4 children: one traces and writes the hours, one tilts the card with the protractor, one points it north, and each child reads the dial at one of the four times.

check.q: A city has a latitude of 27 degrees. How far should the dial card be tilted from flat?
check.why: The tilt of the dial plate from flat is 90 take away the latitude. 90 take away 27 is 63. The gnomon, at right angles to the plate, then points at the Pole Star at a height of 27 degrees.

flow.context: In this step you tilt the dial for your city and point it north.

flow.do: On a sunny day, set up the dial in sunlight. Do this four times in the day, such as at 10, 11, 12 and 1 o'clock. Note the phone time. Read the time where the pencil's shadow falls. Write both in the table. Work out the difference each time.
flow.say: Read the hour line where the middle of the pencil's shadow falls. The edge is a little blurred, so read the middle. What does your phone say? What is the difference?
flow.kid: Read the dial at four times. Write the phone time too. What is the difference?
flow.parent: Expect the dial to differ from the phone by a few minutes up to about 40 minutes in most of India, and the difference changes a little through the year. For the longitude alone, typical gaps are about 10 minutes at Chennai, 20 at Delhi and 40 at Mumbai, with the dial behind the phone. This needs direct sun, so pick another day if it is cloudy, as it often is in the monsoon. There are two reasons. First, India uses one clock time for everyone, set by the Sun at 82.5 degrees east. The Sun is 4 minutes later for each degree you are west of that. Second, the Earth's path is a little oval and its axis tilts, so the Sun runs up to about 16 minutes fast or slow through the year. Kolkata is east and its Sun is earlier. Mumbai and Jaipur are west, and their Sun is later.
flow.context: In this step you compare your dial's time with the phone's time.

flow.do: Look at the table of differences. Ask for what I think, what I saw and why. Then talk about the great dial at Jaipur.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why? The dial at Jaipur is the same design, but 27 metres tall. What do you think its extra size gives?
flow.kid: Say what I think, what I saw and why. What does a big dial give?
flow.parent: A good answer: what I think: a dial tilted at the city's latitude shows the Sun's time, which is a bit different from the phone's. What I saw: the dial and the phone differed by about the same amount at each of the four times. Why: the Earth turns evenly, so the shadow moves evenly, and every place has its own noon. The big dial in Jaipur works the same way. A big dial spreads each minute over a longer distance, so the time can be read more exactly.

check.q: Why does your sundial not agree exactly with your phone's clock?
options: The dial shows the Sun's time at your place, and the phone shows one time for the whole country
check.why: The dial follows the real Sun at your place. The phone follows Indian Standard Time, which is the Sun's time at one place far to the east. Places to the west have a later noon on the phone's clock.

activities.context: In this activity you build a small sundial tilted for your city, the same design as the giant stone Samrat Yantra at Jaipur. It shows why every place has its own Sun time.

activities.title: Wanderer Watch: catch a planet moving among the stars

materials.item: a phone or tablet with a free sky-map app, or the website stellarium-web.org
a window, balcony or terrace with a view of the evening or morning sky
a notebook and a pencil
your own fist, held at arm's length, to measure the sky

activities.safety: Go on to a balcony or terrace only with a grown-up, and never lean over a railing.

schedule.what: Use the app to find which bright planet is in the sky tonight. Find it in the sky and draw it with the stars next to it.
Draw the same patch of sky again, and check whether the planet has moved.
Draw it a third time. Then use the app to speed up time and watch a planet's loop.

activities.record: Draw the same patch of sky on three nights, with the planet and the nearest three stars each time. Write the date under each drawing.

flow.do: Open the sky-map app and set it to tonight. Find a bright planet that is above the horizon in the evening or morning. Go outside and find it. Draw it and the three nearest stars. Measure the gaps in fists.
flow.say: A planet is a wandering star. Let's find one. In the app, find the brightest planet tonight. Then find it in the real sky. What stars are near it? Draw them.
flow.kid: Find a bright planet with the app. Find it in the sky. Draw it with its three nearest stars.
flow.parent: Venus, Jupiter, Saturn and Mars are the planets you can find without a telescope. Which of them is up changes through the year. The app tells you which. Planets shine with a steady light. Stars twinkle. If it is cloudy, try the next night. Check in the app how far the planet is expected to move in a week. If the sky is cloudy for days, or the app shows no bright planet up this week, draw the Moon next to a bright star on three nights instead. The Moon moves a fist or more each night, so the shift is easy to see. Each child draws their own page. One child with a parent: the parent keeps the app open and the child draws. For 2 to 4 children: one finds the planet in the app, one finds it in the sky, one measures gaps, and one draws, and then swap.
flow.context: This is the first step of Wanderer Watch. You find a planet and draw where it is among the stars.

flow.do: Three days later, at the same time, go out and draw the same patch of sky. Compare it with the first drawing. Has the planet moved against the stars? Which way?
flow.say: Three nights later, same time, same place. Where is the planet now? Where are the stars? Which have moved, and which have not?
flow.kid: Draw the same patch again. Has the planet moved against the stars?
flow.parent: Venus moves about a finger-width or two in three days, and Mars about one. Jupiter and Saturn move much less than one finger-width in a week, so they may look unmoved. Measure the gap between the planet and a nearby star in finger-widths at arm's length each night. If you chose a slow planet and see no change, do not worry. Draw it again after three weeks, or trust the app, which shows the small shift. If you cannot see a shift, look at the three nights together. The stars stay put in the drawing and the planet slides.

check.q: Why were planets called 'wanderers' by the Greeks?
options: They change place among the fixed stars from night to night
check.why: Over days and weeks, the fixed stars keep their patterns, but a planet slowly moves against them. That wandering was the puzzle that astronomers worked on for thousands of years.

flow.do: On the seventh night, draw it a third time. Then use the app to speed up time by a month a second. Watch Mars, Jupiter or Saturn for a year. Look for the backward loop.
flow.say: Now the app can show us a whole year in a few seconds. Watch the planet against the stars. Does it ever stop and slide backwards? When?
flow.kid: Speed up time in the app. Watch the planet. Does it slide backwards?
flow.parent: In the app, choose a planet that is far from the Sun, such as Mars or Jupiter. Set the time step to one day. When the planet seems to stop, slide back and go forward again, you have seen retrograde motion. Earth overtakes it, as a car overtakes a lorry.
flow.context: In this step you use the app to watch a planet's backward loop.

flow.do: Look at your three drawings and the loop in the app. Ask for what I think, what I saw and why.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why? Why did people long ago think the planets were wandering stars?
flow.kid: Say what I think, what I saw and why. Why 'wanderers'?
flow.parent: A good answer: what I think: planets move among the stars, and sometimes loop backwards. What I saw: the planet shifted against the stars over a week, and the app showed a backward loop. Why: the planets go round the Sun at different speeds, and from our own moving Earth they seem to wander and loop.

check.q: In the app, Mars seems to slide backwards for a time. What is happening in a Sun-centred picture?
options: The faster Earth is overtaking the slower Mars
check.why: The Earth goes round the Sun faster than Mars does. As the Earth passes Mars, Mars seems to slide back against the stars, as a slower lorry seems to slide back when a car overtakes it.

activities.context: In this activity you draw the same patch of sky over a week, and then use a sky app to watch a planet's loop. It shows why planets were called wanderers.

setup.caption: 1. Find the planet in the app. Then find it in the real sky.

setup.art: A notebook page with three small drawings of the same star patch, a planet in a different place in each.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the same patch on three nights. The planet moves against the stars.

setup.caption: 3. Speed up time in the app and watch the planet's backward loop.

activities.title: Fix the Calendar: why 1900 was not a leap year but 2000 was

materials.item: a sheet of paper and a pencil
a calculator, for checking only
a wall calendar showing a leap year, if you have one

schedule.what: Work out how much a year of 365 days drifts from the Sun's year. Try the rule of a leap year every 4 years. Then find the extra rule that fixes what is left.

activities.record: Make a table of the years 1896, 1900, 1904, 2000, 2024 and 2100, with a tick if each is a leap year.

flow.do: Tell your child that the Sun's year is 365 days, 5 hours and 49 minutes. Ask how far behind a year of exactly 365 days falls. Work it out together, in hours, and then in days over four years.
flow.say: The real year is 365 days and almost 6 hours. If our calendar says 365 days, how many hours behind is it each year? After four years, how many hours? How many days is that?
flow.kid: A year is 365 days and almost 6 hours. How far behind is a calendar of 365 days?
flow.parent: Almost 6 hours a year gives almost 24 hours in four years. That is one day. So adding one day every fourth year nearly fixes it.
flow.context: This is the first step of Fix the Calendar. You work out how much a calendar of 365 days drifts from the Sun's year.

flow.do: Say that a leap year every four years gives an average year of 365 and a quarter days. The extra quarter day is 6 hours. The true year is 11 minutes shorter than that. Work out the drift over one year and over 128 years.
flow.say: A leap year every fourth year makes the calendar year 6 hours longer than 365 days. But the real year is only 5 hours and 49 minutes extra. That leaves 11 minutes too many. How many minutes over 128 years? How many days is that?
flow.kid: The calendar year is 11 minutes too long. How many minutes in 128 years?
flow.parent: 11 times 128 is 1,408 minutes. 1,408 divided by 60 is about 23 and a half hours, which is almost one day. So the calendar gets ahead of the Sun by about a day every 128 years.

check.q: A calendar year is 11 minutes too long. After about how many years is the calendar one day out?
check.why: A day has 1,440 minutes. 1,440 divided by 11 is about 131. So after about 128 to 131 years, the 11 minutes a year have added up to a day.

flow.do: Tell the story: by 1582, the calendar had drifted 10 days from the Sun. Pope Gregory XIII had 10 days removed that year, so 4 October was followed by 15 October. His astronomers added a new rule: a year ending in 00 is a leap year only if it divides by 400. Test the rule on 1900, 2000 and 2100.
flow.say: By 1582 the calendar was ten days out. They skipped ten days. And they added a rule. A century year is a leap year only if it divides by 400. Is 1900 a leap year? 2000? 2100?
flow.kid: Test the rule. Is 1900 a leap year? 2000? 2100?
flow.parent: 1900 does not divide by 400, so it is not a leap year. 2000 divides by 400, so it is. 2100 does not, so it is not. In 400 years, there are 100 leap years under the old rule, and 3 centuries are skipped, so 97.
flow.context: In this step you test the rule of the Gregorian calendar, which we use today.

flow.do: Make the table of years with a tick for each leap year. Work out the average length of a year: 400 years have 365 days each plus 97 extra days. Divide by 400. Then test your own birth year and a grandparent's.
flow.say: In 400 years there are 97 extra days. That is 400 times 365, plus 97, all divided by 400. What is the average year? How close is that to the real one?
flow.kid: 400 years have 97 leap days. Find the average length of a year.
flow.parent: 400 times 365 is 146,000. Add 97 to get 146,097. Divide by 400 to get 365.2425. The real year is about 365.2422. The difference is so small that the calendar drifts by only one day in about 3,000 years. The year length of 365 days 5 hours 49 minutes is a typical rounded figure. One child with a parent: the parent calls out years such as 1800, 1896, 2024, 2100 and 2400, and the child decides and ticks, with the calculator checking only at the end. For 2 to 4 children: work in pairs, one calls a year, the other judges and says why, and the calculator settles any argument. The first pair to judge ten years right wins.

check.q: Was the year 1900 a leap year?
options: No, because it does not divide by 400
Yes, because it is a century year
check.why: 1900 divides by 4, but it is a century year, and century years are leap years only if they divide by 400. 1900 does not, so there was no 29 February that year. The year 2000 did divide by 400, so it was a leap year.

activities.context: In this activity you work out why a calendar needs leap years, and why the rule has two parts. It shows how astronomers kept the calendar in step with the Sun.

setup.caption: 1. Compare the Sun's year and the calendar year on two rulers.

setup.art: A table of years with ticks for leap years, 1896, 1900, 1904, 2000, 2024 and 2100.
setup.caption: 2. Test the rule on each year and tick the leap years.

projects.title: A Pendulum on a Turntable: the idea behind Foucault's proof

materials.item: a lazy Susan or a turntable from the kitchen, about 25 to 30 centimetres across, that turns smoothly. No turntable? Use the seat of a swivel chair that a grown-up turns slowly, or try the hand-held version in step 3
2 stacks of books, each about 40 centimetres tall, to stand on the turntable on opposite sides
a long ruler or a wooden stick to lay across the top of the two stacks
a fishing swivel (a few rupees at a fishing tackle shop or online), or a small steel key ring or a bent paper clip, to hang the thread from
50 centimetres of fine, smooth thread and a nut, a washer or a stack of coins taped together, of about 30 grams, for the weight
masking tape, a pencil and a sheet of paper

projects.safety: Keep the book stacks low enough to stay steady, and tape the ruler down so that it cannot slip. Keep fingers clear of the turntable's edge. The nut or washer is a small part, so keep it away from children under five. If you use a swivel chair, a grown-up holds it and turns it slowly.

schedule.what: Build the frame on the turntable. Start the pendulum swinging. Turn the turntable slowly by hand through a quarter turn. See which way the pendulum swings.

projects.record: Draw the turntable seen from above at four stops of a quarter turn, with the tape line on the turntable and the swing direction of the pendulum.

flow.do: Show your child the turntable, the books and the pendulum. Explain that the books and ruler turn with the turntable, and the pendulum hangs from the ruler. Ask for a guess: when the turntable turns, will the pendulum turn with it? Write the guess and the reason.
flow.say: The pendulum hangs from a frame that sits on the turntable. When I turn the turntable, will the pendulum swing turn round with it, or keep swinging the same way? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: A pendulum on a turntable. When the table turns, will the swing turn too? Why?

ask.q: Why do you think the swing will, or will not, turn with the table?
good: The frame is holding it, so it will turn.
The pendulum will keep swinging the same way.
I am not sure. Let's test.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Most people expect the swing to turn with the frame.
flow.context: This is the first step of the turntable pendulum. You guess before you build.

flow.do: Stand a stack of books on each side of the turntable, with the stacks the same height. Tape the ruler across the tops. Tape the swivel to the middle of the ruler, above the turntable's centre. Hang the thread from the swivel. Tie the weight on at the bottom, so it hangs just above the turntable.
flow.say: Build the frame so the pendulum hangs right above the middle of the turntable. The swivel lets the thread twist without turning the weight. Tape everything down so it cannot slip.
flow.kid: Stack books on both sides. Tape a ruler across. Hang the pendulum from the middle.
flow.parent: The pendulum should hang about 40 centimetres below the ruler. A smooth, fine thread twists less. If the thread is twisty, hold the weight still for a few seconds before you let it go. The swivel is what lets the pendulum keep its swing direction when the frame turns.

check.q: Why does the pendulum hang from a swivel?
options: So the frame can turn without the thread twisting the weight round
check.why: If the thread were fixed, turning the frame would twist the thread, and the twist would push the pendulum round. A swivel lets the top turn freely while the weight carries on in its own direction.

flow.context: In this step you build the frame and hang the pendulum.

flow.do: Tape a line across the turntable, from one stack to the other, and call it the table line. Tape a second line on the floor behind it, in the direction the pendulum will swing. Call it the room line. Start the pendulum swinging gently along the room line. Turn the turntable slowly by hand a quarter turn. Watch the swing.
flow.say: Start the pendulum swinging gently along the room line, without pushing it sideways. Now turn the turntable very slowly, a quarter turn. Does the swing turn with the table? Or does it stay along the room line?
flow.kid: Start the pendulum swinging. Turn the table slowly. Does the swing turn?
flow.parent: Expected: the frame and the table line turn through a quarter turn, but the pendulum keeps swinging along the room line. If the swing turns into an oval or wobbles, release the weight again without pushing it, or use a longer, finer thread. The result may not be perfect, since there is some friction. What matters is that the swing does not turn with the table. If the swing turns along with the table, the pivot is gripping the thread. Use the swivel, a longer and finer thread, or try the hand-held version: hang the thread from a pencil held in your fingers, start a gentle swing along a tape line on the floor, then slowly turn yourself on the spot. The swing keeps its direction while your hand turns. One child with a parent: the parent turns the table and the child watches. For 2 to 4 children: one turns the table, one starts the pendulum, one watches the floor line, and one records, then swap.
flow.context: In this step you turn the turntable and watch what the pendulum does.

flow.do: Draw the four stops of a quarter turn from above. At each stop, draw the table line and the swing direction. Ask for what I think, what I saw and why. Then ask about the Earth.
flow.say: Tell me three things. What do you think now? What did you see that shows it? And why? Now imagine the turntable is the Earth, and the pendulum is Foucault's pendulum in Paris. What would a person standing on the Earth see?
flow.kid: Draw four stops. Say what I think, what I saw and why. What if the table is the Earth?
flow.parent: This is claim, evidence and reasoning. A good answer: what I think: the pendulum keeps swinging in the same direction while the table turns. What I saw: the table line turned a quarter turn, but the swing stayed along the room line. Why: nothing pushed the swing sideways, so it kept its direction. If the table is the Earth, then to a person standing on it the swing seems to turn slowly in the opposite direction. In 1851, Foucault hung a heavy pendulum in Paris and the swing turned round the floor at about 11 degrees an hour, which showed that the floor was turning under it.

check.q: In Foucault's pendulum, the swing seemed to turn slowly round the floor. What did that show?
options: The floor, and the Earth, was turning under the pendulum
check.why: A pendulum keeps its swing direction, as your turntable pendulum did. If the swing seems to turn over the floor, the floor must be turning under it. This showed that the Earth spins.

projects.context: In this project you hang a pendulum from a frame on a turntable and turn the table. It shows the idea of Foucault's pendulum, which proved in 1851 that the Earth spins.

challenges.title: Find North and Noon with Just a Stick and the Sun
challenges.problem: You have no compass and no clock. Using only a straight stick, the Sun, some pebbles or tape and a ruler, find the north-south line and the moment of local noon.
constraints: Use only a straight stick pushed upright into clay, a sheet of paper, tape or pebbles, and a ruler.
Do not use a phone compass or a phone map to find the answer. A phone clock may be used only to check afterwards.
Mark the tip of the shadow at least five times, 15 minutes apart, around the middle of the day.
materials: a straight stick or pencil about 20 centimetres tall, pushed into a ball of clay (use one 30 to 40 centimetres tall from April to August, when the noon Sun is high)
a large sheet of paper or card, taped down in a sunny place
masking tape, a pencil and a ruler
a watch or phone, to measure the 15 minutes only
general: Mark the tip of the shadow every 15 minutes for an hour or more around the middle of the day, and join the marks with a smooth curve.
The shortest shadow shows the Sun at its highest point. The line from the stick's base to the end of the shortest shadow lies north and south.
Local noon is the time when the shadow is shortest.
creative: Draw a circle round the stick's base that passes through a shadow tip in the morning. Find where the afternoon shadow tip crosses the circle. The line that cuts the two marks in half also points north-south.
Make a tiny hole in a card so that a bright spot of Sun, and not a shadow, marks the time.
Repeat the activity a month later and see how the shortest shadow changes.
challenges.your_turn: Set up your stick and mark the shadow tip five times. Find the north-south line and the time of your local noon. Then check it against your phone clock and your sundial.
challenges.safety: Never look at the Sun. Go on to a terrace or balcony only with a grown-up. Do the test in a safe, sunny place.
challenges.context: This is a puzzle that the first sky-watchers had to solve. You find the north-south line and your local noon from one shadow.

setup.art: A stick in a ball of clay on a sheet of paper in sunshine, with a shadow and a small cross at the shadow's tip.
setup.caption: 1. Stand the stick on the paper. Mark the tip of the shadow.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with five crosses in a curve, a line from the stick to the nearest cross and a note 'shortest shadow'.
setup.caption: 2. Mark the tip every 15 minutes. Join the crosses.

flow.do: Stand the stick upright in clay on a sheet of paper in a sunny place, taped down so it cannot move. Mark the stick's base. Mark the tip of its shadow with a cross and write the time.
flow.say: The shadow of a stick moves as the Earth turns. We will mark where the tip of the shadow falls every 15 minutes. Begin about an hour before you think the Sun is highest.
flow.kid: Stand a stick on paper in the Sun. Mark the tip of the shadow. Write the time.
flow.parent: Local noon is between about 11:15 and 13:00 on a phone clock, depending on where you live in India and the time of year. Start by 11:00 so you catch the shortest shadow, and keep marking until the shadow starts to grow longer. Do not move the paper. Near noon from April to August, the shadow of a short stick is only a few centimetres long in much of India, and the tip is hard to mark. Use a taller stick then, or try in October to February. Pick a clear day, because a cloudy monsoon sky hides the shadow. One child with a parent: the parent keeps time and the child marks. For 2 to 4 children: each child takes charge of one or two of the marks, and one reads the clock.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Stick and the Sun challenge. You mark where the shadow's tip falls.

flow.do: Every 15 minutes, mark the tip of the shadow with a cross and write the time. Do this at least five times. Join the crosses with a smooth curve.
flow.say: Mark the tip again. The shadow is changing length and direction. Is it getting shorter or longer? Which way is it turning?
flow.kid: Every 15 minutes, mark the tip. Write the time. Join the crosses.
flow.wait: Mark the tip every 15 minutes for at least an hour.
flow.parent: While you wait, watch the shadow creep. This is the Earth turning under the Sun. You can do other things between the marks. The marks take an hour, but your own work takes only a few minutes of it.

flow.do: Find the cross that is nearest to the stick's base. Draw a straight line from the base through it. This is the north-south line. The time written next to that cross is your local noon.
flow.say: Find the shortest shadow. Draw a line from the stick's base through the tip. That line points north and south. The time of that cross is your local noon. Compare it with 12 o'clock on your phone.
flow.kid: Find the shortest shadow. Draw a line from the base through it. Compare the time to your phone.
flow.parent: If the shortest shadow falls between two crosses, draw the curve and read the nearest point to the base. Your local noon will differ from 12:00 by up to about an hour, from your place and the time of year. Because the shadow length changes slowly near noon, your local noon may be wrong by 10 or 15 minutes, and the north line by a few degrees. That is normal. A mark every 10 minutes helps.

check.q: When is the shadow of a stick shortest in the day?
options: At local noon, when the Sun is highest
check.why: The Sun is highest at local noon, so it shines down more steeply and makes the shortest shadow. At sunrise and sunset the Sun is low and the shadow is long.

flow.do: Compare your answer with a phone compass and with the sundial if you have made one. Ask: how close were you? What might have made your line a little wrong?
flow.say: How close was your line to the phone compass? What might have made it a little wrong? The stick, the paper, the way you marked the tip?
flow.kid: Check against a compass. How close were you?
flow.parent: A well-done stick shadow finds north to within a few degrees. Mistakes come from a wobbly stick, a blurred shadow tip, and paper that moved. The blurred shadow edge is because the Sun is a disc.

challenges.title: Make Your Case: Earth-centred or Sun-centred? Choose your year
challenges.problem: It is the year 1600. You are a court astronomer. You must advise the king which model of the sky to use: Ptolemy's Earth-centred model, Tycho's middle model, or Copernicus's Sun-centred model. Then you are asked again in 1620, in 1700 and in 1840, and you must see whether your advice changes.
constraints: Use only evidence that was known by the year you are advising in.
Write down what each piece of evidence fits and what it does not.
Give a reason for your choice that a king could understand.
Be fair to the other models.
materials: a sheet of paper and a pencil
a table with four columns, one for each year, drawn by you
the evidence list below, read out by a grown-up
general: 1600: planets loop (all three models explain it), no star shifts are seen (a problem for a moving Earth), Tycho's careful readings exist.
1620: Galileo has seen moons of Jupiter and phases of Venus, so Ptolemy's Venus is wrong. Kepler's ellipses fit the planets' paths well.
1700: Newton's law of gravity explains Kepler's ellipses, and says that a heavy Sun should be at the centre.
1840: Bessel has measured a star's shift, and the Earth's motion is proved. Foucault's pendulum follows in 1851.
creative: Argue as a person who dislikes new ideas, and explain what you would need to see to be persuaded.
Write a letter from a young astronomer to an older one, explaining why the 8 arcminutes matter.
Make a timeline poster showing each piece of evidence at its year and which models it helps.
challenges.your_turn: Write your advice for each of the four years in one or two sentences. Say which piece of evidence made you change your mind, if any.
challenges.context: This is a thinking challenge. You weigh the evidence that astronomers had in different years, and see how the best answer changed.

setup.art: A table with four columns, labelled 1600, 1620, 1700 and 1840, each with a short list of evidence.
setup.caption: 1. Draw the table and list the evidence for each year.

setup.art: A child at a desk with a quill pen writing advice to a king, with a tick next to one model in each column.
setup.caption: 2. Write your advice for each year.

flow.do: Read the problem and the three models. Read out the evidence list for 1600. Ask which model your child would advise, and why. Write the answer.
flow.say: It is 1600. Planets loop, no star seems to shift, and Tycho has careful readings. Which model would you advise the king to use, and why?
flow.kid: It is 1600. Which model would you choose? Why?

ask.q: What evidence helps you decide in 1600?
good: No star shifts, which is a problem for a moving Earth.

flow.parent: In 1600, the evidence could not settle the argument. All three models fitted the loops. The lack of any star shift favoured a still Earth. Many wise people advised Tycho's middle model.
flow.context: This is the first step of Make Your Case. You advise a king in the year 1600.

flow.do: Read the evidence for 1620, 1700 and 1840 one at a time. After each, ask whether the advice changes, and why. Write each answer.
flow.say: Now it is 1620. Galileo has seen the phases of Venus and the moons of Jupiter. Does your advice change? Why? And in 1700, with Newton? And in 1840, with Bessel?
flow.kid: New evidence for 1620. Does your advice change? Why?
flow.parent: Expected: in 1620 Ptolemy's model is out, but Tycho's still fits. In 1700 the Sun-centred model fits Newton best. In 1840, the Earth's motion is proved. A good answer says why the evidence changes things, and does not merely say that the Sun-centred model was right all along. One child with a parent: the parent plays the king and asks why each time. For 2 to 4 children: in 1600, each child argues for one model (Ptolemy, Tycho or Copernicus), and at each new year each says whether to keep it, with the parent reading the evidence and acting as king. Bessel measured his star shift in 1838, so it was known by 1840.

flow.do: Look at your four answers. Talk about what made the most difference, and what a person in 1600 could not have known.
flow.say: Which piece of evidence changed the answer most? Was a person in 1600 foolish to prefer Tycho's model?
flow.kid: Which evidence changed things most?

check.q: In 1600 many wise people chose Tycho's model over Copernicus's. What is the best reason?
options: The evidence of that time did not yet prove that the Earth moves, and no star shift had been seen
They did not care about evidence
They had not heard of Copernicus
check.why: In 1600 no one had seen a star shift as the Earth moved, and nobody could feel the Earth move. Tycho's model fitted all the sky as well. Choosing it was reasonable on the evidence of the time.

worksheets.title: Who Moves? Earth, Sun and Planets (core)

items.p: A passenger in a smooth train shuts her eyes. Why can she not tell whether the train is moving?
opts: A steady movement cannot be felt, only changes in movement
Her body is too heavy to feel it
items.why: Our bodies feel starts, stops and turns, not steady movement. This is why nobody could feel the Earth turn.

items.p: With your eyes shut in the spinning chair, a slow steady turn was hard to feel, but a sudden stop was easy. Explain why.
items.a: The body senses changes in movement. A steady turn has no change to feel. A sudden stop is a big change, so it can be felt.
items.why: A strong answer says that the body feels changes in movement and not steady movement, and uses both halves of the test.

items.p: Aryabhata wrote that the stars only seem to move west because the ____ turns to the east.
items.why: Aryabhata's picture was a boat: a person in a boat moving forward sees the bank moving backwards.

items.p: A planet going round the Earth in a plain circle would sometimes slide backwards among the stars.
items.why: False. A planet on a plain circle round us would always move the same way. Backward loops needed something extra, such as Ptolemy's small circles, or the Earth overtaking the planet.

items.p: In a Sun-centred picture, why does Mars seem to slide backwards for a time?
opts: The faster Earth is overtaking the slower Mars
items.why: The Earth goes round the Sun faster than Mars does. As the Earth passes Mars, Mars seems to slide back against the stars, as a slower lorry seems to slide back when a car passes it.

items.p: Match each word to its meaning.
pairs: Having the Earth at the centre
Having the Sun at the centre
A stretched circle with two special points inside
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These four words are used all through the story of how astronomers changed their minds.

items.p: In the lamp-and-ball test, a ball that stayed between you and the lamp never looked more than a thin crescent. What does that tell you about Ptolemy's Venus?
items.a: In Ptolemy's model Venus stays between the Earth and the Sun. Then it could only show crescents. Galileo saw Venus nearly full, so Ptolemy's model could not be right.
items.why: A strong answer links what the ball did to what Galileo saw, and says the model could not make a full Venus.

items.p: Put these steps of Kepler's discovery in order, from first to last.
items: Kepler finds that a circle misses by 8 arcminutes
Tycho measures Mars very carefully for many years
Kepler throws out the circle and finds the ellipse
Kepler tries circle after circle for Mars
a: Tycho measures Mars very carefully for many years
Kepler tries circle after circle for Mars
Kepler finds that a circle misses by 8 arcminutes
Kepler throws out the circle and finds the ellipse
items.why: The careful readings came first. The trial of circles showed a small gap, and a careful scientist trusted the gap more than the circle.

items.p: What is an ellipse?
opts: A stretched circle, like an oval, with two special points inside
items.why: A circle is a special ellipse with both special points in the same place. Planets move on ellipses with the Sun at one of the two points.

items.p: Sort these ideas. Does each one put the Earth at the centre or the Sun at the centre?
items: Ptolemy's model
Earth at the centre
Copernicus's model
Sun at the centre
Aristarchus's idea from about 250 BCE
Sun at the centre
the idea that the Sun, Moon and planets all go round us
Earth at the centre
items.a: see items
items.why: Ptolemy and the plain Earth-centred picture put us in the middle. Aristarchus and Copernicus put the Sun there.

items.p: Galileo's telescope proved beyond doubt that the Earth goes round the Sun.
items.why: False. The telescope showed that Ptolemy's Venus was wrong, but Tycho's middle model also fitted. The proof that the Earth moves came much later, from star shifts and pendulums.

items.p: Draw an ellipse that you made with two pins. Mark the two pins and label one of them 'Sun'.
items.a: An oval with two dots inside it on the long line, one of them labelled Sun.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the Sun at one of the two points, and not in the middle of the oval.
items.art: A blank page with a faint line across the middle.

items.p: Your sundial says noon when your phone says 12:20. What is the best reason?
opts: The sundial shows the Sun's time at your place, and the phone shows one time for the whole country
items.why: Each place has its own noon, because the Earth turns. The phone follows Indian Standard Time, set by the Sun far to the east. Places to the west see their noon later on the phone.

items.p: A sundial is tilted from flat by 90 degrees take away the ____ of its city.
items.why: The tilt makes the dial parallel to the equator. Then the shadow turns evenly, 15 degrees every hour.

items.p: Why is the edge of the shadow on a sundial blurred?
items.a: The Sun is a round disc and not a point. Each point on the disc makes its own shadow, and they overlap in the middle and slide apart at the edge. So the edge fades.
items.why: A strong answer says that the Sun is a disc, and that each point of it casts its own shadow.

items.p: Label the picture of a quadrant: straw sight, scale, thread, weight.
items.a: The straw is along the flat edge. The scale is the curved edge with numbers. The thread hangs from the centre mark. The weight is at the end of the thread.
items.why: A strong labeller puts the thread at the centre of the scale and the weight at its bottom end, because the weight keeps the thread straight down.
items.art: A drawing of a card with a half-circle protractor, a straw and a hanging thread, with four blank label lines.

items.p: The Earth is farther from the Sun in January than in July.
items.why: False. The Earth is a little closer to the Sun in early January. The seasons come from the tilt of the Earth's axis, and not from the distance.

items.p: Which set of readings of an angle has the higher precision?
items.why: Precision means that repeated readings agree. The first set lies between 26 and 28. The second set is spread over 15 degrees.

items.p: In 1543, Copernicus said that the Sun is at the centre. His model was no more accurate than Ptolemy's. Three people are discussing whether he was right to suggest it.

views.says: He was right to suggest it. An idea can be right before there is proof, and his picture explained why planets loop.
I would keep Ptolemy's tables. If the Earth moves, we should see the stars shift, and nobody has.
Both matter. Use the better tables for work, and keep testing the new idea to see if it explains more.

items.ask: Which person do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then say one thing that another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer picks a side and gives a reason, such as the idea explaining loops simply, or the lack of any star shift. It then admits a fair point from another side.
items.why: This is a real question about how to treat new ideas that are not yet proved. Each view has a good point.

items.p: Why is it so hot across India in May, when the Earth is not closer to the Sun then?
opts: The tilt of the Earth's axis makes the Sun climb higher and the days longer
The Earth is closer to the Sun in May
items.why: The Earth is actually nearest to the Sun in early January. Seasons come from the tilt of the axis, which changes how high the Sun climbs.

items.p: Explain Aryabhata's boat in your own words, and say what it has to do with the Sun seeming to move.
items.a: A person in a boat moving forward sees the still things on the bank moving backwards. In the same way, we are on the turning Earth and see the still stars and Sun moving the other way across the sky.
items.why: A strong answer says that our own movement makes the world seem to move the other way.

items.p: Venus looks the same size all the time through a telescope.
items.why: False. Venus looks about six times wider when it is nearest to us than when it is farthest. When nearest, it is a big thin crescent.

items.p: Kepler found that a planet moves ____ when it is closer to the Sun.
items.why: The Sun's pull is stronger when the planet is nearer, so the planet speeds up, and slows down when it is far.

items.p: Your best spread of readings with the quadrant is 1 degree. How many arcminutes is that?
items.why: One degree has 60 arcminutes. Tycho's readings were good to about 1 arcminute, 60 times more precise.

items.p: Tycho's middle model also explained the phases of Venus. So why was it still important that Galileo saw them?
items.a: The phases showed that Venus goes round the Sun, and not the Earth. That ruled out Ptolemy's model, which had been used for 1,400 years. It did not decide between Tycho's and Copernicus's models, but it narrowed the choices.
items.why: A strong answer says what the evidence ruled out as well as what it left open.

items.p: Put these in order of size, smallest first.
items: 1 degree
1 arcminute
the width of the Moon in the sky
8 arcminutes
a: the width of the Moon in the sky
items.why: The Moon is about 30 arcminutes wide, which is half a degree. So 1 arcminute, then 8, then 30, then 60 arcminutes in one degree.

items.p: Draw the lamp and the ball. Show where the ball must be to look nearly full when seen from the chair.
items.a: A lamp in the middle, a chair on one side, and a ball on the far side of the lamp from the chair, a little off the line.
items.why: A strong drawing puts the ball beyond the lamp, so that the lit half faces the viewer.
items.art: A blank page with a lamp drawn in the middle and a chair on the left.

items.p: Would a passenger with her eyes shut feel each of these?
items: a train starting suddenly
Feels it
a train braking hard
Feels it
a smooth steady speed
Does not feel it
the Earth turning at Chennai
Does not feel it
a sharp corner
Feels it
items.a: see items
items.why: We feel changes in movement. A steady speed or turn gives the body nothing to sense.

items.p: Brahmagupta doubted that the Earth moved. What was one of his reasons?
opts: A bird flying up from a tree would not find the tree again
The Earth is too heavy to move
items.why: He thought that if the ground raced away, things would be left behind. We now know that the air and birds move along with the Earth, just as a fly in a smooth train moves with the train.

items.p: A student says that Copernicus's model was simply better because it was simpler. What would you add?
items.a: Copernicus still used circles and small extra circles, so his tables were no more accurate than Ptolemy's. The Sun-centred model won later, because Kepler, Galileo and Newton gave it better maths and evidence.
items.why: A strong answer says that simpler is not enough on its own, and that evidence decided it.

items.p: Planets move fastest when they are farthest from the Sun.
items.why: False. A planet moves fastest when it is closest to the Sun. Far planets also take longer to go round.

items.p: Why did Jai Singh build his observatories of stone and not brass?
opts: Stone does not bend or wear, so the scales keep their shape
items.why: Thin brass instruments warped and wore with time. A stone instrument keeps its shape, and being big allows a finer scale.

items.p: Match each piece of evidence to what it showed.
pairs: A long pendulum's swing slowly turns over the floor
A star shifts a tiny amount during the year
A gap of 8 arcminutes from the best circle
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each of these needed careful instruments, and each changed what astronomers believed.

items.p: Cecilia Payne was told her result was impossible, but she was right. What should a careful scientist do when a new result seems wrong?
items.a: Check the work and the method, ask others to repeat it, and be open to the possibility that it is right. Do not reject a result only because it surprises you or because of who found it.
items.why: A strong answer says to check the evidence, and not to dismiss it because it is new or comes from an unexpected person.

items.p: Kolkata is east of Jaipur. Which has local noon first?
opts: Kolkata, because the Sun reaches the east first
They have noon at the same moment
items.why: The Earth turns towards the east, so the Sun reaches places in the east first. Kolkata has its noon nearly an hour before Jaipur.

items.p: Mars seems to slide backwards when the Earth ____ it.
items.why: The Earth is on the faster, inner track. It passes Mars as a car passes a lorry.

items.p: A sundial tilted wrongly for its city still shows even hours.
items.why: False. Only a dial tilted at the city's latitude has its plate parallel to the equator, so that the shadow turns evenly. A wrongly tilted dial reads some hours too fast and others too slow.

items.p: Give three reasons why a thoughtful person in 1600 could still doubt that the Earth moves.
items.a: Nobody could feel the Earth move. No star seemed to shift, which a moving Earth should cause. The Sun-centred model was no more accurate than the old one. Also, Tycho's middle model explained the sky as well.
items.why: A strong answer gives reasons that fitted the evidence of the time, and does not treat people of 1600 as foolish.

items.p: The careful readings of a planet's place differ by a tiny amount from the shape of a perfect circle. Three people are discussing what to do.

views.says: My instruments are careful. If the readings differ from the circle by even a tiny amount, we should trust the readings.
A circle is the most beautiful shape. A tiny difference is probably a mistake in the readings.
Before choosing, test the readings again. If they hold up, the circle must go, however beautiful it is.

items.ask: Which idea do you agree with most? Give a reason from this unit. Then say one thing that another person has right.
items.a: A strong answer uses Kepler and the 8 arcminutes: the readings had been tested and were more reliable than the circle. It then admits that a difference can sometimes be a mistake, so the readings should be checked first.
items.why: This is how Kepler decided. It balances trust in careful measurement against love of a beautiful idea.

items.p: A pendulum is set swinging at the North Pole. About how long does its swing take to turn once all the way round the floor?
items.why: At the pole, the floor turns once all the way round in about 24 hours under the pendulum. So the swing seems to turn once round in a day. Near the equator it would hardly turn at all.

items.p: You draw an ellipse with a 24 centimetre loop and the pins 6 centimetres apart. About how wide is it?
items.why: The loop's length is the pin distance plus the width, so the width is 24 take away 6, which is 18 centimetres.

items.p: Why would a gap of 8 arcminutes be invisible with your quadrant but plain to see with Tycho's?
items.a: My quadrant's readings were spread over a degree or more, which is 60 arcminutes. Eight arcminutes is hidden inside that spread. Tycho's readings were good to about one arcminute, so eight stood out clearly.
items.why: A strong answer compares the gap with the spread of readings.

items.p: The Earth's path round the Sun is so close to a circle that a 20 centimetre drawing of it would differ from a circle by less than a millimetre.
items.why: True. The Earth's path is only a tiny bit off a circle. The stretched ovals in books are drawn that way on purpose, to show the idea.

items.p: Under the rule for leap years that we use now, how many leap days are there in 400 years?
items.why: There would be 100 leap years if every fourth year counted. Three century years, which do not divide by 400, are skipped, so there are 97.

items.p: Put these steps of finding a star's distance by parallax in order.
items: Compare the two positions and measure the tiny shift
Look at the star in January and mark its place among the others
Work out the distance from the size of the shift
Look at it again in July, when the Earth is on the other side of the Sun
a: Look at the star in January and mark its place among the others
Look at it again in July, when the Earth is on the other side of the Sun
Compare the two positions and measure the tiny shift
Work out the distance from the size of the shift
items.why: Parallax uses two viewpoints, as two eyes do. The Earth's journey gives two views six months apart, and the smaller the shift, the farther the star.

items.p: Draw the Sun with two orbits round it, the Earth on the inner orbit and Mars on the outer one. Show where the Earth is when it overtakes Mars.
items.a: The Sun in the middle with a small orbit and a larger orbit. The Earth and Mars are on the same side of the Sun, with the Earth on the inner orbit between the Sun and Mars.
items.why: A strong drawing shows Earth between the Sun and Mars, which is when Mars seems to slide back.
items.art: A blank page with a dot for the Sun in the middle.

items.p: Is each of these better explained by the Earth's spin or by the Earth's journey round the Sun?
cats: The Earth's journey round the Sun
items: day and night
The Earth's spin
the Sun rising in the east
The Earth's spin
Mars's backward loops
The Earth's journey round the Sun
a star's tiny yearly shift
The Earth's journey round the Sun
different constellations in the evening sky through the year
The Earth's journey round the Sun
items.a: see items
items.why: The spin takes a day and explains rising and setting. The journey takes a year and explains things that repeat through the year.

items.p: At the equator the ground moves at about 1,670 kilometres an hour with the Earth's spin. How fast does the ground move at the North Pole?
opts: Hardly at all, just turning on the spot
items.why: Right at the pole, the ground just turns once a day on the spot. The farther from the pole, the bigger the circle, and the faster the ground moves.

items.p: Explain how a stone dial in Jaipur can say noon while a phone says 12:27, and both can be right.
items.a: The dial shows the Sun's time at Jaipur, and noon there is when the Sun is highest. The phone shows Indian Standard Time, set by the Sun far to the east. The Earth turns eastwards, so the Sun reaches Jaipur about 27 minutes later than that eastern place. Each clock answers a different question.
items.why: A strong answer says that the two clocks measure different things, and uses the turn of the Earth.

items.p: Indian Standard Time is the same as the Sun's time at Chennai.
items.why: False. Indian Standard Time is based on the Sun at 82.5 degrees east, and Chennai is at about 80.3 degrees east. The Sun is at its highest in Chennai about 9 minutes later than at the standard place, before adjusting for the time of year.

items.p: The two special points inside an ellipse are called ____.
items.why: Each planet goes round the Sun on an ellipse, with the Sun at one of the foci.

items.p: Which of these would most have convinced a critic in 1543 that the Earth goes round the Sun?
opts: Seeing a star shift a tiny amount over the year
Seeing the Sun rise in the east
items.why: A moving Earth should make the nearer stars shift against the farther ones. The Sun rising and Mars looping were explained by every model. The shift was the missing proof, and it was first measured in 1838.

items.p: Pick one old idea about the sky that turned out to be wrong, and say how it was shown to be wrong.
items.a: One example: planets move on perfect circles. Kepler used Tycho's careful readings of Mars and found that the best circle was wrong by 8 arcminutes. He trusted the readings, gave up the circle and found an ellipse. Another example: Ptolemy's Venus, which Galileo's telescope showed was wrong.
items.why: A strong answer names the idea, the evidence that showed it wrong, and how the evidence was gathered.

quiz.p: A cup of tea stays steady on a tray in a smooth aeroplane flying at 800 kilometres an hour. What does this show about steady movement?
opts: A steady movement does not disturb things or feel like anything
Aeroplanes are made to hold tea cups
quiz.why: Only changes in movement are felt. A smooth steady speed leaves everything inside as if it were still. This is why we do not feel the Earth turn.

quiz.p: Why does the Sun seem to move across the sky from east to west?
opts: The Earth turns towards the east, so the Sun seems to go the other way
The Sun goes round the Earth once a day
The sky is a turning bowl
quiz.why: The Earth turns once a day. We turn with it and do not feel it, so the Sun seems to cross the sky in the opposite direction, as the bank seems to slide backwards from a boat.

quiz.p: Why did Ptolemy add small circles to the paths of the planets?
opts: To explain why planets seem to slide backwards for a time
To make the paths look pretty
quiz.why: A plain circle round the Earth cannot make a planet go backwards. A small circle riding on a big one can, and Ptolemy's tables worked well enough for over a thousand years.

quiz.p: In a Sun-centred picture, what happens when Mars seems to slide backwards?
opts: The Earth is passing Mars on the inside track
Mars is slowing to a stop
Mars is turning round the Earth
quiz.why: The Earth is on the faster, inner track and overtakes Mars. From the passing Earth, Mars seems to slide back against the stars.

quiz.p: In the lamp-and-ball test, a ball that stays between you and the lamp can look only like what?
quiz.why: The lamp lights the half of the ball that faces the lamp. If the ball stays in front of the lamp, you mostly see the dark half.

quiz.p: Galileo saw Venus look nearly full and small, and later look like a big thin crescent. What did this show?
opts: Venus goes round the Sun and not only in front of it
quiz.why: A nearly full Venus must be seen from the far side of its path, and that is beyond the Sun. Ptolemy's model could not do this.

quiz.p: Resting the quadrant on a table made the readings agree more closely than holding it in the hands. What is the reason?
opts: The table took away the shaking of the hands
The table made the sticker bigger
The table made the numbers smaller
quiz.why: A shaking hand scatters the readings. A steady rest makes each reading nearly the same as the last, which is higher precision.

quiz.p: Why did Tycho Brahe build huge, steady brass instruments?
opts: A bigger instrument has a bigger scale that can be read more finely
Because small ones were not allowed
quiz.why: On a larger scale, one arcminute is a few millimetres long and can be read. A steady, fixed instrument also reduces the scatter of readings.

quiz.p: What is the shape of the path of a planet round the Sun?
opts: An ellipse, with the Sun at one of the two special points
A perfect circle with the Sun in the middle
quiz.why: Kepler found this from Tycho's readings of Mars. For most planets, the ellipse is so close to a circle that only careful readings show the difference.

quiz.p: What made Kepler give up circles for the path of Mars?
opts: The best circle missed Tycho's careful readings by 8 arcminutes
He saw Mars through a telescope
quiz.why: Kepler trusted Tycho's readings, which were never wrong by that much, more than the beauty of a circle. He followed the gap and found an ellipse.

quiz.p: A sundial in Chennai and one in Delhi need different tilts. Why?
opts: The tilt must match each city's latitude, so the dial lies parallel to the equator
quiz.why: Only a dial parallel to the equator has a shadow that turns evenly, 15 degrees every hour. The tilt from flat is 90 take away the latitude, which differs from city to city.

quiz.p: The Jaipur sundial says noon when the phone says 12:27. Why do they differ?
opts: The dial shows Jaipur's own Sun time, and the phone shows one time for all of India
quiz.why: Each place has its own noon, because the Earth turns. Indian Standard Time is set by the Sun far to the east, so the Sun reaches Jaipur later on that clock.

quiz.p: In 1925, Cecilia Payne found what the stars are mostly made of. What was it?
quiz.why: She used the dark lines in starlight and an equation by the Indian physicist Meghnad Saha. She showed that stars are mostly hydrogen and helium, though she was told at first that this was impossible.

applications: Phone maps use the same idea of two viewpoints as parallax and the same geometry as Kepler's ellipses, to place satellites and find your position.
Spacecraft are aimed using Kepler's ellipses and Newton's gravity, as Mangalyaan was aimed at Mars.
Standard time zones are set so that every place on Earth has a clock that is roughly in step with the Sun.
Surveyors use the same angle-measuring idea as the quadrant, in an instrument called a theodolite, to map land and plan roads.
Navigators on ships once used the astrolabe and later the sextant to find their latitude from the height of the Sun or the Pole Star.
The leap-year rule keeps farmers, festivals and school terms in step with the seasons.
A Foucault pendulum in a science museum shows visitors that the Earth turns.
Astronomers still check old records, such as Chinese and Babylonian eclipse notes, to measure how the Earth's spin has slowed over thousands of years.
Sundials and sun-tracking panels both use the idea of pointing at the Sun with a tilt that matches the latitude.
Spectrum lines, first read in starlight, are used today to find the metals in an old pot, a gemstone or a river sample.

open_questions.q: Who first thought that the Earth might move?
open_questions.why_open: Ideas about a moving Earth appear in Greece, India and the Islamic world, but old writings are lost or hard to date. Nobody knows who thought of it first.

open_questions.q: How did astronomical ideas travel between India, the Islamic world and Europe?
open_questions.why_open: Some books were translated and some tables were copied, but for many ideas nobody has found the exact road they took.

open_questions.q: What were the old stone circles and mounds really for?
open_questions.why_open: Many line up with the Sun or the Moon, but without written records we cannot be sure the builders meant them to.

open_questions.q: How many women astronomers were forgotten?
open_questions.why_open: Many women worked as assistants, calculators and instrument makers, and their names were not always written down. Historians are still finding more.

open_questions.q: Why does a model that is wrong still sometimes give right answers?
open_questions.why_open: Ptolemy's circles gave good tables for over a thousand years. Philosophers of science still discuss what it means for a model to be true or useful.

open_questions.q: Is there any experiment that could tell steady motion from standing still?
open_questions.why_open: Physicists have found none so far. Whether that means standing still has no meaning is still discussed.

open_questions.q: How much did the sky-watchers of the past know that we have not yet found in their records?
open_questions.why_open: Thousands of old astronomy books and tablets in India, the Middle East and elsewhere have not been read or translated.

maths.problem: Your best spread of quadrant readings is 2 degrees. Tycho's readings were good to 1 arcminute. There are 60 arcminutes in a degree. How many times more precise was Tycho than your quadrant?
maths.explain: 2 degrees is 2 times 60, which is 120 arcminutes. 120 arcminutes compared with 1 arcminute is 120 times.
maths.context: In Tycho's Quadrant, you found the spread of your readings and changed it into arcminutes.
maths.why_maths: Changing degrees into arcminutes lets you compare your own readings with Tycho's on the same scale.

maths.problem: India's Standard Time is set by the Sun at 82.5 degrees east. Chennai is at about 80.3 degrees east. The Sun is 4 minutes later for every degree you go west. How many minutes later is the Sun's noon in Chennai than at the standard place?
maths.explain: 82.5 take away 80.3 is 2.2 degrees. 2.2 times 4 is 8.8 minutes, which is about 9 minutes.
maths.context: In the sundial activity, your dial and your phone disagreed by a few minutes.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying the degrees by 4 minutes shows why a sundial and a phone differ, and by how much.

maths.problem: Jaipur is at about 75.8 degrees east. Standard time is set at 82.5 degrees east. The Sun is 4 minutes later for every degree you go west. By about how many minutes does the Sun reach its highest point at Jaipur after it did at the standard place?
maths.explain: 82.5 take away 75.8 is 6.7 degrees. 6.7 times 4 is 26.8, which is about 27 minutes.
maths.context: In the story at the Jaipur observatory, the dial said noon when the phone said twenty-seven minutes past twelve.
maths.why_maths: The same calculation explains the gap in the story, and shows that it was not a mistake.

maths.problem: The Earth's circumference at the equator is about 40,000 kilometres, and it turns once in 24 hours. About how fast does the ground move at the equator? A very fast Indian train runs at about 160 kilometres an hour. How many times faster is the ground?
maths.answer: About 1,670 kilometres an hour, which is about 10 times as fast as the train.
maths.explain: 40,000 divided by 24 is about 1,667. 1,667 divided by 160 is about 10.4. So the ground moves about 10 times faster than the train, and we do not feel it.
maths.context: In the explanation of why a steady turn cannot be felt, the ground at the equator moves at a great speed.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the distance by the time shows how fast we are really moving without feeling it.

maths.problem: With a loop of thread 24 centimetres round, the width of an ellipse is 24 take away the distance between the pins. How wide is the shape with the pins 6 centimetres apart? How wide with 12 centimetres apart? What is the pin distance for a width of 20 centimetres?
maths.explain: 24 take away 6 is 18. 24 take away 12 is 12. For a width of 20, the pins must be 24 take away 20, which is 4 centimetres apart.
maths.context: In the ellipse drawing, you moved the pins apart and measured the widths.
maths.why_maths: Seeing the rule between the pin distance and the width lets you predict a shape before you draw it.

maths.problem: A calendar year with a leap year every fourth year is 11 minutes too long. How many minutes too long is it after 128 years? How many hours is that, and how close is it to one day?
maths.answer: 1,408 minutes, about 23 and a half hours, which is almost one day.
maths.explain: 11 times 128 is 1,408. 1,408 divided by 60 is about 23.5 hours. One day is 24 hours, so it is nearly a whole day.
maths.context: In Fix the Calendar, you worked out how a small error in the year grows over time.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying a small error by many years shows how it grows into a whole day, and why the calendar needed a new rule.

maths.problem: Under the Gregorian rule, 400 years have 97 leap days. How many days are in 400 years? What is the average length of a year?
maths.answer: 146,097 days, and an average year of 365.2425 days.
maths.context: In Fix the Calendar, you tested the rule for leap years that we use today.
maths.why_maths: Finding the average year shows how close the rule is to the true length of the year.

maths.problem: In the spinning chair test, a child answered six rounds and got four right. If she had just guessed each round, she would expect to get three right. By how much did she beat chance? Is that enough to be sure she could feel the turn?
maths.answer: She beat chance by one round. That is not enough to be sure.
maths.explain: 4 take away 3 is 1. With only six rounds, getting one more than chance can easily happen by luck. To be sure, you would need many more rounds.
maths.context: In the Spinning Chair test, you scored six rounds with the eyes shut.
maths.why_maths: Comparing your score with what chance would give tells you whether a result is worth trusting.

maths.problem: Venus is about 40 million kilometres from the Earth when it is nearest, and about 260 million kilometres when it is farthest. About how many times farther away is it when farthest? What does that suggest about how its size changes?
maths.answer: About 6 times farther, so it looks about 6 times wider when nearest.
maths.explain: 260 divided by 40 is 6.5. A thing that is 6.5 times farther looks about 6.5 times smaller across. So Venus looks about 6 times wider when it is nearest.
maths.context: In Galileo's Venus, the ball looked big when near and small when far.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the two distances shows how much the size of Venus changes, which is what Galileo saw.

maths.problem: The Earth overtakes Mars about every 780 days. A month is about 30 days. About how many months is that? If Mars was last overtaken in March, in which season of the year will the next overtaking be?
maths.answer: About 26 months, so it will be about two years and two months later, in May.
maths.explain: 780 divided by 30 is 26 months. 26 months is 2 years and 2 months. Two months after March is May.
maths.context: In the explanation of the wandering stars, Mars's backward loop happens about every 26 months.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the days by a month's length changes a long count of days into a time you can picture, and lets you predict the next loop.

maths.problem: The Samrat Yantra at Jaipur is about 27 metres tall. You make a model of it that is 100 times smaller. How tall is the model in centimetres?
maths.explain: 27 metres is 2,700 centimetres. 2,700 divided by 100 is 27 centimetres.
maths.context: In the sundial activity, your small dial is a model of the great Jaipur dial.
maths.why_maths: Dividing by the scale shrinks a huge instrument to a model you can build.

maths.problem: At Paris, Foucault's pendulum turned its swing by about 11 degrees every hour. About how many hours would it take to turn all the way round, through 360 degrees?
maths.explain: 360 divided by 11 is about 32.7. So it would take about 33 hours to turn all the way round.
maths.context: In the turntable pendulum project, you saw how a pendulum keeps its swing while the table turns.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the full turn by the hourly turn tells you how long the whole turn takes, which can be checked against a real pendulum.

how_we_found_out.story: For about 2,000 years, nearly every astronomer believed that the planets must move in perfect circles, because the circle seemed the perfect shape for the heavens. Ptolemy used circles, and so did Copernicus. Tycho Brahe, a Danish nobleman, spent twenty years measuring the places of planets with huge brass instruments, to about one arcminute, before any telescope existed. After Tycho died in 1601, Johannes Kepler used his readings of Mars. For years he tried one circle after another. At last he found one that matched Tycho's readings to within 8 arcminutes. That is about a quarter of the width of the Moon in the sky. Kepler knew that Tycho's readings were never wrong by that much. He wrote that he could not ignore those 8 arcminutes. He threw out his circle. Then he tried an oval, and it fitted. In 1609 he published his result: Mars goes round the Sun on an ellipse, with the Sun at one of its two foci.
how_we_found_out.who: Johannes Kepler, a German astronomer (1571 to 1630), using the readings of Tycho Brahe, a Danish astronomer (1546 to 1601)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Astronomers believed for 2,000 years that planets must move on perfect circles. Kepler showed that a circle misses the real readings by 8 arcminutes, and that the path is an ellipse.

playtest: Read as a parent and child in a city flat would use it, but not yet tried at home. The Spinning Chair needs a chair that turns smoothly and a quiet room, and the results will be near chance for many children, which is part of the lesson. If there is no swivel chair, a stool on a thick cloth on a smooth floor can be turned by a grown-up. Galileo's Venus needs a dark evening room and a bright LED, and works well because a ball that stays in front of the lamp can only show a crescent. The quadrant readings depend on a steady stand and a clear sticker. The sundial needs a sunny day, a phone compass and some patience, and the shadow may fall on the back face in winter, which is why both faces are marked. The turntable pendulum needs a fine thread and a swivel, and may not be perfect, since the swing can drift. Facts for a grown-up to check: Mariam al-Asturlabi's dates, the dates of the Jantar Mantars, Ulugh Beg's star count, the Venus distances and the 11 degrees an hour at Paris.
